question_text: Are higher-graded CBP Officers leaving at a higher rate than lower grades?
answer_text:
Exploratory

No. Among CBP Officers, the highest grades (12 to 15) do not leave faster than the grades below them. Grades 12 and 13, which hold about four-fifths of the cell, separated at about 0.032 over the twelve months to August 2026, below the cell's overall 0.035. The fastest-leaving grades are the lower ones: grade 05 at 0.102 and grade 07 at 0.077. Grade 15 (0.066) and grade 14 (0.038) are above grades 12 and 13, but they are small groups of about 180 and 850. Late reports keep arriving, so these rates will rise slightly. No separations in these grades carry the 2025 deferred resignation program flag, so the rates with and without that wave are the same. Headcount in grades 05 and 07 rose sharply over the year, so the average of the two snapshots is only an approximation there.

| Grade | Separation rate | Separations | Average headcount |
|---|---|---|---|
| 00 | 0.2188 | 7 | 32 |
| 05 | 0.1023 | 67 | 655 |
| 07 | 0.0773 | 81 | 1,049 |
| 09 | 0.0395 | 61 | 1,545 |
| 11 | 0.0067 | 8 | 1,198 |
| 12 | 0.0317 | 550 | 17,325 |
| 13 | 0.0315 | 136 | 4,313 |
| 14 | 0.0376 | 32 | 850 |
| 15 | 0.0663 | 12 | 181 |

Rate is separations divided by the average of the August 2025 and August 2026 headcounts. I read "higher-graded" as grades 12 to 15 against grades 05 to 11, for CBP Officers, over the trailing twelve months to August 2026; if you meant a different period, or the count of separations rather than the rate, say so.

```sql
with hc as (
  select grade,
         sum(case when snapshot_month = '2025-09-01' then 1 else 0 end) as start_n,
         sum(case when snapshot_month = '2026-08-01' then 1 else 0 end) as end_n
  from semantic.workforce_snapshot
  where agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD'
    and occupational_series_code = '1895'
    and snapshot_month in ('2025-09-01', '2026-08-01')
  group by grade
),
sep as (
  select grade,
         count(*) as sep_n,
         count(*) filter (where drp_indicator = 'Y') as drp_n
  from semantic.separation
  where agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD'
    and occupational_series_code = '1895'
    and effective_month between '2025-09-01' and '2026-08-01'
  group by grade
)
select coalesce(hc.grade, sep.grade) as grade,
       coalesce(hc.start_n, 0) as headcount_start,
       coalesce(hc.end_n, 0) as headcount_end,
       coalesce(sep.sep_n, 0) as separations,
       coalesce(sep.drp_n, 0) as separations_drp
from hc
full outer join sep on sep.grade = hc.grade
order by grade
```

question_text: Roughly how many CBP Officers could retire in the next five years, going by age bracket and years of service?
answer_text:
Exploratory

About 10,660 CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) could reach retirement eligibility by August 2031, out of 27,650 on the August 2026 snapshot (38.6%). Of those, 5,760 (20.8%) already qualify on age and service. This is an eligibility count, not a forecast of departures, and the data holds no retirement-plan field, so the rule is my assumption: age 50 with 20 years of service.

The count is an upper bound. It adds 2,245 officers aged 45 to 49 with 20 or more years, 1,325 aged 50 or older with 15 to under 20 years, and 1,330 aged 45 to 49 with 15 to under 20 years, all of whom would cross both thresholds inside the window. Officers with under 15 years are excluded. I read this as CBP Officers on the August 2026 snapshot with a five-year window; if you meant the retirement separations actually recorded for this cell, or a different eligibility rule, say so.


answer_text:
Verified
Assuming, as you state, that no one could be onboarded from October 1 to November 12, 2025, the plan scaled to the days hiring was possible is about 316 hires, and the 475 actual accessions land +158.6 hires (+50.1%) against it. The full-quarter comparison was -119 hires (-20.0%) against the plan of 594.

- Days in the quarter: October 1 to December 31, 2025 = 31 + 30 + 31 = 92
- Days hiring could not happen: October 1 to November 12 = 31 + 12 = 43
- Days hiring was possible: 92 - 43 = 49
- Scaled plan: 594 x 49 / 92 = 316.4
- Variance against the scaled plan: 475 - 316.4 = +158.6, or 158.6 / 316.4 = +50.1%

The scaling does not explain the shortfall; it only shows that the comparison flips sign under your assumption. Accessions actually recorded for October to December 2025 are the better test of whether anyone was onboarded in that window, and I can pull them by month with a one-off query if you want. Later OPM files can also add accessions. I read this as the same cell and quarter with the plan prorated for the stated window; the full-quarter comparison is the nearest alternative.

question_text: TSA told Congress about 1,110 screeners left during the October and November 2025 shutdown. What does the OPM data show, and how many of those were quits?
answer_text:
Exploratory
The OPM data shows 1,041 TSA screeners (Compliance Inspection and Support, 1802) separated in October and November 2025, of whom 702 (about 67%) were quits. That is 69 fewer than the 1,110 TSA reported to Congress, and I can't tell from the data why the two figures differ. Late reports keep arriving, so these counts may grow slightly, and only 4 of the 1,041 came through the 2025 deferred resignation program.

Breakdown by separation category: quits 702; other separation 182; voluntary retirement 126; individual transfer out 21; other retirement 10. I added the five categories to get the 1,041 total.

I read "screeners" as the TSA 1802 cell, all separation categories, effective October and November 2025; if you meant all TSA occupations, or the 1,110 figure's basis, say so.

```sql
SELECT separation_category, COUNT(*) AS separations, SUM(CASE WHEN drp_indicator = 'Y' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS drp_separations FROM semantic.separation WHERE agency_subelement_code = 'HSBC' AND occupational_series_code = '1802' AND effective_month BETWEEN '2025-10-01' AND '2025-11-01' GROUP BY separation_category ORDER BY separations DESC
```

question_text: What's the average salary of TSA screeners, and how does it compare with CBP Officers?
answer_text:
Exploratory

TSA screeners (Compliance Inspection and Support, 1802) had an average annualized basic pay of $74,752 as of the August 2026 snapshot, about $29,759 (roughly 40%) below the $104,511 average for CBP Officers (1895). Basic pay is estimated for almost all of both groups: 42,225 of 46,913 TSA screener rows and all 27,650 CBP Officer rows carry imputed pay, filled in from job postings because OPM redacted it. These are averages of basic pay only, not total compensation. I read "average salary" as average annualized basic pay at the August 2026 snapshot; if you meant a different month or total pay, say so.

```sql
SELECT agency_subelement_code, agency_subelement, occupational_series_code, occupational_series, COUNT(*) AS headcount, ROUND(AVG(annualized_adjusted_basic_pay)::numeric, 0) AS avg_basic_pay, SUM(CASE WHEN pay_imputed THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS pay_imputed_rows FROM workforce_snapshot WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01' AND agency_subelement_code IN ('HSBC', 'HSBD') AND occupational_series_code IN ('1802', '1895') GROUP BY agency_subelement_code, agency_subelement, occupational_series_code, occupational_series ORDER BY agency_subelement_code, occupational_series_code
```

answer_text:

889 USAJOBS postings listed Border Patrol Agent (series 1896) among their occupational series, with open dates from September 1, 2025 to October 31, 2026. question_text: Do higher-grade CBP Officer postings stay open longer than lower-grade ones?
answer_text:
Exploratory

Lower-grade CBP Officer postings stay open longer, not shorter. Postings advertised at grades 5 to 9 averaged about 25 days open (36 postings), against about 7 days for postings at grades 11 to 15 (428 postings), for announcements opened September 2025 to October 2026.

Average days open, by minimum grade (close date minus open date):

| Minimum grade | Postings | Average days open |
|---|---|---|
| 5 to 9 (combined) | 36 | 25.1 |
| 11 to 15 (combined) | 428 | 7.3 |

Grade 00 (6 postings, about 13 days) is left out because those rows are senior executive postings, not a grade band. The posting table does not carry a component field, so these are all postings listing the 1895 series, not only CBP's. A posting's window shows how long it was advertised, not how long a hire took; there are no applicant records, so time to hire is not available. I read "higher-grade" as the posting's minimum grade and "stay open" as its advertised window; if you meant the maximum grade, or postings still open on a given date, say so.

```sql
SELECT minimum_grade, maximum_grade, COUNT(*) AS postings, ROUND(AVG(close_date - open_date), 1) AS avg_days_open, MIN(close_date - open_date) AS min_days_open, MAX(close_date - open_date) AS max_days_open FROM semantic.job_posting WHERE occupational_series_codes ? '1895' AND open_date BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-10-31' GROUP BY minimum_grade, maximum_grade ORDER BY minimum_grade, maximum_grade
```

question_text: How many CBP Officers who left this year had less than one year of service?

Exploratory

138 CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) with under one year of service left between January and August 2026, the calendar year to date. That is out of 591 separations in the period. Over the trailing twelve months (September 2025 to August 2026) the count is 170, 32 of them in September to December 2025. None of the under-one-year separations came through the 2025 deferred resignation program. Late reports keep arriving, so these counts will grow. The counts do not depend on location, but every separation row's duty station is estimated from job postings, not published by OPM. I read "this year" as calendar 2026; if you meant the trailing twelve months, the figure is 170.

question_text: Are higher-graded CBP Officers leaving at a higher rate than lower grades?
answer_text:
Exploratory

No. CBP Officers in grades 13 to 15 separated at 0.0337 over the twelve months to August 2026, against 0.0352 for grades 5 to 12, so the senior grades are not leaving faster. Grade 15 looks higher at 0.0663, but that rests on 12 separations, so treat it as noise. The highest rates are in the lowest grades (5, 7, and 00), and grade 00 rests on only 7 separations.

| Grade | Separations | Average headcount | Rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| 00 | 7 | 32 | 0.2188 |
| 05 | 67 | 655 | 0.1023 |
| 07 | 81 | 1,049 | 0.0773 |
| 09 | 61 | 1,545 | 0.0395 |
| 11 | 8 | 1,198 | 0.0067 |
| 12 | 550 | 17,325 | 0.0317 |
| 13 | 136 | 4,313 | 0.0315 |
| 14 | 32 | 850 | 0.0376 |
| 15 | 12 | 181 | 0.0663 |

The 2025 deferred resignation program wave contributes no separations in any grade of this cell, so the rate is the same with and without it. Late reports keep arriving, so these counts will grow slightly. Rates are separations divided by the average of the September 2025 and August 2026 headcounts. This is a one-off query, not a standard calculation, so the grade split is not verified against the review's standard figures.

I read "higher-graded" as grades 13 to 15 against grades 5 to 12, trailing twelve months to August 2026; if you meant a single grade or the count of separations, say so.

```sql
SELECT grade, COUNT(*) AS separations, SUM(CASE WHEN drp_indicator = 'Y' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS drp_separations FROM semantic.separation WHERE effective_month BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-01' AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895' GROUP BY grade ORDER BY grade
```

question_text: How many postings listed the Border Patrol series 1896 between September 2025 and October 2026, counting ones that list several series?
answer_text:
Exploratory

I found 889 USAJOBS announcements that list Border Patrol Agent (series 1896) and were opened between September 1, 2025 and October 31, 2026, across all of DHS. Every one of those 889 lists only series 1896, so none of them is a multi-series posting that the count would otherwise have had to add. Each announcement has a distinct control number, so 889 is 889 separate postings. This is a count of postings, not of hires; the records do not link postings to the people hired through them.

I read this as announcements opened in that window, for all components, counting any posting that lists 1896 among its series; if you meant postings open on a particular date, say so and I will use the open-postings calculation instead.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS posting_rows, COUNT(DISTINCT control_number) AS distinct_control_numbers, SUM(CASE WHEN occupational_series_codes ? '1896' AND jsonb_array_length(occupational_series_codes) > 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS multi_series_rows FROM semantic.job_posting WHERE occupational_series_codes ? '1896' AND open_date >= DATE '2025-09-01' AND open_date <= DATE '2026-10-31'
```

question_text: Do higher-grade CBP Officer postings stay open longer than lower-grade ones?
answer_text:
Exploratory

No. Lower-grade CBP Officer postings stayed open longer, not shorter. Across the 470 CBP Officer (1895) announcements opened September 2025 to October 2026, grade 7 and grade 9 postings averaged about 29 days from open to close, while grades 11 to 15 averaged 6 to 8 days. These are advertised windows, not time to fill: the data has no applicant or hire link, so it cannot show how long a vacancy stayed unfilled. Postings filled or cancelled early are not visible, so the true open period may differ. Some grade 13 and 14 postings ran as long as 181 to 183 days, which pulls their maximum up even though their average is short. Six postings state no grade (recorded as "00", about 13 days) and are left out of the comparison.

I read "higher grade" as the maximum grade listed and "stay open" as the advertised open-to-close window; if you meant the minimum grade or time to hire, say so.

```sql
SELECT maximum_grade, COUNT(*) AS postings, ROUND(AVG(close_date - open_date), 1) AS avg_open_days, MIN(close_date - open_date) AS min_open_days, MAX(close_date - open_date) AS max_open_days FROM semantic.job_posting WHERE occupational_series_codes ? '1895' AND open_date BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-10-31' GROUP BY maximum_grade ORDER BY maximum_grade
```

question_text: When in the year do CBP Officers retire? Show retirements by month.
answer_text:
Exploratory

CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) retired most often in December 2025, with 152 of their 586 retirements in the twelve months from September 2025 to August 2026 (about 26%). Outside December, the monthly count ran between 24 and 54 through the rest of the period, and the months after December were mostly between 26 and 52. Late reports keep arriving, so the most recent months, especially August 2026, will grow.

| Month | Retirements |
|---|---|
| 2025-09 | 54 |
| 2025-10 | 36 |
| 2025-11 | 24 |
| 2025-12 | 152 |
| 2026-01 | 44 |
| 2026-02 | 26 |
| 2026-03 | 31 |
| 2026-04 | 45 |
| 2026-05 | 52 |
| 2026-06 | 46 |
| 2026-07 | 45 |
| 2026-08 | 31 |

These are counts of retirement separations (voluntary, early out, and other), not rates, and the records do not give a reason for them. I read this as retirement counts by effective month for CBP Officers over the twelve months to August 2026; if you meant the retirement rate or the whole calendar year, say so.

```sql
SELECT effective_month, COUNT(*) AS retirements
FROM semantic.separation
WHERE agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD'
  AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
  AND effective_month BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-01'
  AND separation_category LIKE 'RETIREMENT%'
GROUP BY effective_month
ORDER BY effective_month
```

question_text: Are higher-graded CBP Officers leaving at a higher rate than lower grades?
answer_text:
Exploratory

No. Over the twelve months to August 2026, CBP Officers at GS-13 and above separated at a rate of 0.034 (180 separations on an average headcount of about 5,344), against 0.049 for GS-5 to GS-11 (217 separations on about 4,446). GS-12, the largest grade with about 17,300 on average, separated at 0.032. The highest rates are at the lower grades, GS-5 (0.102) and GS-7 (0.077). GS-15 is higher than the other senior grades at 0.066, but that rests on 12 separations, and the Senior Executive rows (0.219 on about 32 people) are too small to read.

The 2025 deferred resignation wave does not touch this cell: no separation in the window carries its flag, so the rate is the same with and without it. Late reports keep arriving, so counts will grow slightly. Grade is as recorded at each snapshot, and promotions during the year move people between grades, so the grade-level rates are approximate.

I read "higher-graded" as GS-13 and above, and the measure as the trailing twelve-month separation rate to August 2026. If you meant separation counts by grade, or a different grade cut, say so.

```sql
WITH seps AS (
  SELECT pay_plan_code, grade, COUNT(*) AS separations, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE drp_indicator IS DISTINCT FROM 'Y') AS separations_excl_drp
  FROM semantic.separation
  WHERE effective_month BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-01' AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
  GROUP BY pay_plan_code, grade
),
hs AS (
  SELECT pay_plan_code, grade, COUNT(*) AS hc_start
  FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
  WHERE snapshot_month = '2025-09-01' AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
  GROUP BY pay_plan_code, grade
),
he AS (
  SELECT pay_plan_code, grade, COUNT(*) AS hc_end
  FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
  WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01' AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
  GROUP BY pay_plan_code, grade
)
SELECT COALESCE(seps.pay_plan_code, hs.pay_plan_code, he.pay_plan_code) AS pay_plan_code,
       COALESCE(seps.grade, hs.grade, he.grade) AS grade,
       COALESCE(hs.hc_start, 0) AS hc_start,
       COALESCE(he.hc_end, 0) AS hc_end,
       COALESCE(seps.separations, 0) AS separations,
       COALESCE(seps.separations_excl_drp, 0) AS separations_excl_drp,
       ROUND(COALESCE(seps.separations, 0) / NULLIF((COALESCE(hs.hc_start, 0) + COALESCE(he.hc_end, 0)) / 2.0, 0), 4) AS rate,
       ROUND(COALESCE(seps.separations_excl_drp, 0) / NULLIF((COALESCE(hs.hc_start, 0) + COALESCE(he.hc_end, 0)) / 2.0, 0), 4) AS rate_excl_drp
FROM seps
FULL OUTER JOIN hs ON hs.pay_plan_code = seps.pay_plan_code AND hs.grade = seps.grade
FULL OUTER JOIN he ON he.pay_plan_code = COALESCE(seps.pay_plan_code, hs.pay_plan_code) AND he.grade = COALESCE(seps.grade, hs.grade)
ORDER BY pay_plan_code, grade
```

question_text: Roughly how many CBP Officers could retire in the next five years, going by age bracket and years of service?
answer_text:
Exploratory

About 10,660 CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895), roughly 39% of the 27,650 on the August 2026 snapshot, reach age 50 with 20 years of service within five years. About 5,760 of them already meet that test today. The records hold no retirement eligibility field, so this uses a proxy I chose: age 50 with 20 years of service. Actual federal retirement rules differ, and eligibility is not the same as retirement, so treat this as a ceiling on the pool, not a forecast. Age and service are reported in bands, so the 15-to-19-year cut is approximate.

- Already at age 50 or older with 20+ years: 2,483 + 2,130 + 850 + 297 = 5,760
- Aged 45 to 49 with 20+ years (reach 50 within five years): 2,245
- Aged 45 or older with 15 to 19.99 years (reach 20 within five years): 1,330 + 767 + 333 + 176 + 49 = 2,655
- Total: 5,760 + 2,245 + 2,655 = 10,660; 10,660 / 27,650 ≈ 0.386

I read this as CBP Officers on the August 2026 snapshot, five-year horizon from August 2026, using age 50 with 20 years of service as the retirement test. If you meant the retirements actually recorded over the last twelve months, say so and I can pull those by separation category.

```sql
SELECT age_bracket,
       CASE WHEN length_of_service_years < 10 THEN 'under 10 years'
            WHEN length_of_service_years < 20 THEN '10 to 19 years'
            ELSE '20 years or more' END AS service_band,
       COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01'
  AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD'
  AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2
```

```sql
SELECT age_bracket,
       CASE WHEN length_of_service_years >= 20 THEN '20 years or more'
            WHEN length_of_service_years >= 15 THEN '15 to 19.99 years'

       COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01'

  AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
  AND age_bracket IN ('45-49', '50-54', '55-59', '60-64', '65 OR MORE')
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2
```

Assuming, as you state, that no one could be onboarded from October 1 to November 12, 2025, the plan scaled to the days hiring was possible is about 316 hires. - Days hiring could not happen: October 1 to November 12 = 31 + 12 = 43
- Days hiring was possible: 92 - 43 = 49
- Scaled plan: 594 x 49 / 92 = 316.4, about 316

question_text: What's the average salary of TSA screeners, and how does it compare with CBP Officers?
answer_text:

TSA screeners (Transportation Security Administration, series 1802) averaged about $74,752 in annualized basic pay as of the August 2026 snapshot, against about $104,511 for CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, series 1895). That is a gap of $29,759, or about 40% more for CBP Officers. Every city figure is estimated, not published by OPM: the duty station was filled in from job postings, which show where CBP hires rather than where officers sit. The masking test covered only FEMA and CISA, where the drawn state matched the true state 11% and 28% of the time; for CBP, whose staff spread across hundreds of ports and border crossings, that test flatters the method. I read this as the duty-station cities of CBP Officers at the August 2026 snapshot; if you meant another month or the state totals, say so.

```sql
SELECT duty_station_city, duty_station_state, COUNT(*) AS headcount, SUM(CASE WHEN location_imputed THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS imputed_rows FROM workforce_snapshot WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01' AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895' GROUP BY duty_station_city, duty_station_state ORDER BY headcount DESC LIMIT 50
```

question_text: Do higher-grade CBP Officer postings stay open longer than lower-grade ones?
answer_text:
Exploratory
No. Higher-grade CBP Officer postings have shorter posted windows, not longer ones. Across the 469 CBP Officer (1895) announcements opened September 1, 2025 to October 31, 2026, the average gap between open and close date was about 29 days at GS-07 and GS-09, and 6 to 8 days at GS-11 to GS-15.

| Maximum grade | Postings | Average days open | Median days open |
|---|---|---|---|
| GS-07 | 13 | 29.2 | 30 |
| GS-09 | 14 | 29.3 | 30 |
| GS-11 | 3 | 8.0 | 6 |
| GS-12 | 62 | 8.3 | 6 |
| GS-13 | 210 | 7.3 | 6 |
| GS-14 | 129 | 6.1 | 6 |
| GS-15 | 32 | 6.4 | 6 |
| No numbered grade (00) | 6 | 13.3 | 13 |

The records hold only the posted open and close dates, not the date each posting was filled, so these figures show how long each announcement was advertised, not how long it stayed open in practice or how long hiring took. The GS-13 range runs from 4 to 181 days, so one long announcement moves that average.

I read "stay open longer" as the posted window (close date minus open date) for all CBP Officer postings opened in the coverage period, grouped by maximum grade. If you meant postings still open on August 1, 2026, or grouping by minimum grade, say so.

```sql
SELECT maximum_grade AS grade, COUNT(*) AS postings, ROUND(AVG(close_date::date - open_date::date), 1) AS avg_days_open, percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY close_date::date - open_date::date) AS median_days_open, MIN(close_date::date - open_date::date) AS min_days, MAX(close_date::date - open_date::date) AS max_days FROM semantic.job_posting WHERE agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_codes ? '1895' AND open_date::date BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-10-31' GROUP BY maximum_grade ORDER BY maximum_grade
```

question_text: Are higher-graded CBP Officers leaving at a higher rate than lower grades?
answer_text:
Exploratory

No. For CBP Officers (CBP, 1895), the separation rate in the twelve months to August 2026 is highest at the lower grades, not the higher ones. Grade 05 is at 0.102 and grade 07 at 0.077, against 0.032 for grade 12, the largest group at about 17,000 officers. Grades 13 and 14 sit close to grade 12, at 0.032 and 0.038. Grade 15 is higher at 0.066, but it rests on 12 separations against about 180 officers, so treat it as noise.

| Grade | Headcount Sep 2025 | Headcount Aug 2026 | Separations | Rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 05 | 412 | 898 | 67 | 0.102 |
| 07 | 863 | 1,234 | 81 | 0.077 |
| 09 | 1,429 | 1,661 | 61 | 0.040 |
| 11 | 1,125 | 1,270 | 8 | 0.007 |
| 12 | 17,520 | 17,130 | 550 | 0.032 |
| 13 | 4,251 | 4,375 | 136 | 0.032 |
| 14 | 834 | 866 | 32 | 0.038 |
| 15 | 174 | 188 | 12 | 0.066 |

Across the whole cell, 954 separations over a mean headcount of about 27,147 gives 0.035 (954 ÷ 27,147). No separation in this cell carries the deferred resignation flag, so the rate with and without that wave is the same. Grade 05 headcount roughly doubled over the year, so its rate is less stable, and grade 00 (36 staff, 7 separations) is too small to read. Late reports keep arriving, so these counts will grow slightly. Grade is not an estimated field here; this reading uses no estimated location or pay.

I read this as the trailing twelve-month separation rate by grade for CBP Officers to August 2026; if you meant the count of separations, or a different month, say so.

```sql
WITH hc AS (
  SELECT grade,
         SUM(CASE WHEN snapshot_month = DATE '2025-09-01' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS headcount_start,
         SUM(CASE WHEN snapshot_month = DATE '2026-08-01' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS headcount_end
  FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
  WHERE agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD'
    AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
    AND snapshot_month IN (DATE '2025-09-01', DATE '2026-08-01')
  GROUP BY grade
),
sep AS (
  SELECT grade,
         COUNT(*) AS separations,
         SUM(CASE WHEN drp_indicator = 'Y' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS separations_drp
  FROM semantic.separation
  WHERE agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD'
    AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
    AND effective_month BETWEEN DATE '2025-09-01' AND DATE '2026-08-01'
  GROUP BY grade
)
SELECT COALESCE(hc.grade, sep.grade) AS grade,
       hc.headcount_start,
       hc.headcount_end,
       sep.separations,
       sep.separations_drp,
       ROUND(sep.separations::numeric / NULLIF((hc.headcount_start + hc.headcount_end) / 2.0, 0), 4) AS rate,
       ROUND((sep.separations - sep.separations_drp)::numeric / NULLIF((hc.headcount_start + hc.headcount_end) / 2.0, 0), 4) AS rate_excl_drp
FROM hc
FULL OUTER JOIN sep ON hc.grade = sep.grade
ORDER BY grade
```

question_text: Roughly how many CBP Officers could retire in the next five years, going by age bracket and years of service?
answer_text:
Exploratory

About 8,005 CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) could be retirement-eligible within five years, as of the August 2026 snapshot: 5,760 are already aged 50 or older with 20 or more years of service, and another 2,245 aged 45 to 49 with 20 or more years will reach age 50 by 2031. That is about 29% of the 27,650 CBP Officers on the August 2026 rolls.

- The eligibility threshold (age 50 with 20 years) is my assumption from the standard law-enforcement retirement rule. The records have no eligibility flag, so treat this as an upper bound on eligibility, not a forecast of departures.
- The 5,760 includes 297 officers aged 65 or older. The 1,518 aged 50 or older with 10 to 20 years are not counted, although some will reach 20 years within five years.
- Age and service are published OPM values, not estimated.
- I read this as the count of CBP Officers who could retire within five years as of August 2026, using the 50-and-20 threshold. If you meant the retirements actually taken in the past twelve months, I can pull those by category.

```sql
SELECT age_bracket,
       CASE WHEN length_of_service_years < 1 THEN '<1'
            WHEN length_of_service_years < 3 THEN '1-3'
            WHEN length_of_service_years < 5 THEN '3-5'
            WHEN length_of_service_years < 10 THEN '5-10'
            WHEN length_of_service_years < 20 THEN '10-20'
            ELSE '20+' END AS service_bucket,
       COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01'
  AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD'
  AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2
```

question_text: TSA told Congress about 1,110 screeners left during the October and November 2025 shutdown. What does the OPM data show, and how many of those were quits?
answer_text:
Exploratory
The OPM data show 1,041 separations of TSA screeners (Compliance Inspection and Support, 1802) with effective dates in October and November 2025: 541 in October and 500 in November. Of those, 702 were quits (372 in October and 330 in November), about 67% of the total. The figure TSA gave Congress, 1,110, is 69 higher than the OPM count, and the data does not show how TSA counted, so I could not reconcile the two. Separation counts can still be restated in later files (about 0.8% of records), and the data holds categories, not reasons for leaving.

I read "screeners" as TSA's 1802 series, counting every separation category as a separation and quits as the QUIT category, with and without the 2025 deferred resignation program flag. If TSA's 1,110 covers all TSA occupations rather than screeners alone, say so and I can pull that total.

```sql
SELECT effective_month, separation_category, drp_indicator, COUNT(*) AS separations FROM semantic.separation WHERE effective_month >= '2025-10-01' AND effective_month <= '2025-11-01' AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBC' AND occupational_series_code = '1802' GROUP BY effective_month, separation_category, drp_indicator ORDER BY effective_month, separation_category, drp_indicator
```

question_text: What's the average salary of TSA screeners, and how does it compare with CBP Officers?
answer_text:
Exploratory

On the August 2026 snapshot, TSA screeners (Transportation Security Administration (HSBC), Compliance Inspection and Support, 1802) average $74,752 in annualized basic pay across 46,913 staff. CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection (HSBD), 1895) average $104,511 across 27,650 staff, about $29,759 (roughly 40%) more. Both averages are estimated: pay was imputed from job postings for 42,225 of the TSA screener rows (about 90%) and for all CBP Officer rows, because OPM redacted them. The screener figure also includes CBP's own 1802 staff (1,958 people, average $57,418), which I left out of the TSA line.

```sql
SELECT agency_subelement_code, agency_subelement, occupational_series_code, occupational_series, COUNT(*) AS headcount, ROUND(AVG(annualized_adjusted_basic_pay)::numeric, 0) AS avg_basic_pay, SUM(CASE WHEN pay_imputed THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS pay_imputed_rows FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01' AND agency_subelement_code IN ('HSBC', 'HSBD') AND occupational_series_code IN ('1802', '1895') GROUP BY agency_subelement_code, agency_subelement, occupational_series_code, occupational_series ORDER BY agency_subelement_code
```

question_text: How many postings listed the Border Patrol series 1896 between September 2025 and October 2026, counting ones that list several series?

question_text: Do higher-grade CBP Officer postings stay open longer than lower-grade ones?
answer_text:
Exploratory
No. In CBP Officer (1895) announcements opened September 2025 to October 2026, the higher-grade postings closed fastest. Grades 12 to 15 had a median posting window of 6 days (averages of 6.4 to 7.7 days), while grade 5 had a median of 30 days (average 29.3) and grade 9 a median of 28 days (average 22.4). Grade 00 (6 postings) had a median of 13 days, and grade 11 has a single posting at 6 days. These are posting windows, from open date to close date, not time to hire, since the records cannot link postings to the people hired through them. The query covered every announcement listing the 1895 series; I did not confirm that all of them are CBP postings. I read "stay open longer" as the posting window by minimum grade; if you meant time to hire, the records do not hold that.

```sql
SELECT minimum_grade, COUNT(*) AS postings, percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY close_date - open_date) AS median_days_open, ROUND(AVG(close_date - open_date), 1) AS avg_days_open FROM semantic.job_posting WHERE occupational_series_codes ? '1895' AND open_date >= '2025-09-01' AND open_date <= '2026-10-31' GROUP BY minimum_grade ORDER BY minimum_grade
```

question_text: When in the year do CBP Officers retire? Show retirements by month.
answer_text:
Exploratory
CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) retired 586 times in the twelve effective months September 2025 to August 2026. December 2025 was the peak at 152, about 26% of that total, and the other eleven months ran between 24 and 54 a month, with a smaller rise in April and May 2026 (45 and 52).
Late reports keep arriving, so the most recent months (June to August 2026) will grow. The counts include all three retirement categories (voluntary, early out, and other) and do not separate out the 2025 deferred resignation program wave.
I read "when in the year" as the calendar month of retirement across the trailing twelve months; if you meant a single fiscal year or only voluntary retirements, say so.

```sql
SELECT effective_month, COUNT(*) AS retirements FROM semantic.separation WHERE agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895' AND separation_category LIKE 'RETIREMENT%' AND effective_month BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-01' GROUP BY effective_month ORDER BY effective_month
```

question_text: Which DHS components lost the most senior executives this year?
answer_text:
Exploratory

DHS Headquarters lost the most senior executives (57 separations), followed by FEMA (44), ICE (37), and CBP (31), for the twelve months from September 2025 to August 2026. The 2025 deferred resignation program accounts for 15 of Headquarters' 57 and 23 of FEMA's 44; ICE and CBP had none. TSA recorded no senior executive separations in that window.

| Component | Senior executive separations | Of which deferred resignation |
|---|---|---|
| DHS Headquarters (HSAA) | 57 | 15 |
| FEMA (HSCB) | 44 | 23 |
| ICE (HSBB) | 37 | 0 |
| CBP (HSBD) | 31 | 0 |
| USCIS (HSAB) | 30 | 9 |
| CISA (HSCA) | 27 | 7 |
| U.S. Secret Service (HSAD) | 23 | 0 |
| S&T (HSFA) | 8 | 5 |
| U.S. Coast Guard (HSAC) | 7 | 1 |
| FLETC (HSBE) | 4 | 0 |
| Domestic Nuclear Detection Office (HSDA) | 3 | 1 |
| OIG (HSAE) | 2 | 1 |

These are counts, not rates, so large components will naturally show more separations. I read "senior executives" as the Senior Executive Service pay plan (ES) and "this year" as the twelve months of separations in the data, September 2025 to August 2026; if you meant calendar 2026 only, or a rate against headcount, say so.

```sql
SELECT agency_subelement_code, agency_subelement, COUNT(*) AS senior_executive_separations, SUM(CASE WHEN drp_indicator = 'Y' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS drp_separations, SUM(CASE WHEN drp_indicator = 'Y' THEN 0 ELSE 1 END) AS separations_excl_drp FROM semantic.separation WHERE effective_month BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-01' AND pay_plan_code = 'ES' GROUP BY agency_subelement_code, agency_subelement ORDER BY senior_executive_separations DESC
```

```sql
WITH hc AS (
  SELECT grade,
         COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE snapshot_month = '2025-09-01') AS start_n,
         COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01') AS end_n
  FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
  WHERE agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
    AND snapshot_month IN ('2025-09-01', '2026-08-01')
  GROUP BY grade
),
sp AS (
  SELECT grade,
         COUNT(*) AS seps,
         COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE drp_indicator = 'Y') AS drp_seps
  FROM semantic.separation
  WHERE agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
    AND effective_month BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-01'
  GROUP BY grade
)
SELECT COALESCE(hc.grade, sp.grade) AS grade,
       hc.start_n, hc.end_n, sp.seps, sp.drp_seps,
       ROUND(sp.seps / ((hc.start_n + hc.end_n) / 2.0), 4) AS rate,
       ROUND((sp.seps - sp.drp_seps) / ((hc.start_n + hc.end_n) / 2.0), 4) AS rate_excl_drp
FROM hc FULL JOIN sp ON hc.grade = sp.grade
ORDER BY 1
```

question_text: Roughly how many CBP Officers could retire in the next five years, going by age bracket and years of service?
answer_text:
Exploratory

Roughly 11,400 of the 27,650 CBP Officers (about 41%) reach retirement eligibility at some point by August 2031 under the approximation below. About 6,200 of them are already eligible as of the August 2026 snapshot, and the rest become eligible within five years. The records hold no retirement-eligibility field, so I applied a common law-enforcement retirement approximation: 25 years of service at any age, or 20 years at age 50 or older. Check that against the retirement rules that apply to these officers before quoting it. Eligibility is not the same as retiring; the separation categories show how many retirements actually happened.

| Group (August 2026 snapshot) | Headcount |
|---|---|
| Already eligible: 25+ years, any age | 3,371 |
| Already eligible: 20 to 24 years, age 50 or older | 2,822 |
| Become eligible within five years: 20 to 24 years, under 50 | 2,539 |
| Become eligible within five years: 15 to 19 years, age 45 or older | 2,655 |
| **Total eligible by August 2031** | **11,387** |

I read "could retire" as eligibility under that approximation, with the August 2026 snapshot as the starting point; if you meant the count of retirement separations in the trailing twelve months, say so.

```sql
SELECT age_bracket,
       CASE WHEN length_of_service_years < 10 THEN 'under 10 years'
            WHEN length_of_service_years < 20 THEN '10 to under 20 years'
            ELSE '20 or more years' END AS service_band,
       COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01'
  AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD'
  AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2
```

```sql
FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01'
  AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD'
```

question_text: How many postings listed the Border Patrol series 1896 between September 2025 and October 2026, counting ones that list several series?
answer_text:
Exploratory

889 job postings listed the Border Patrol Agent series (1896) among their series, counting every posting that lists it alongside others. These are announcements opened from September 1, 2025 through October 31, 2026, across all of DHS. Each posting has a distinct control number, so none is double-counted. Postings show where DHS advertises, not who was hired through them, and the count is of announcements, not openings. question_text: Do higher-grade CBP Officer postings stay open longer than lower-grade ones?
answer_text:
Exploratory

No. Across the 470 CBP Officer (series 1895) postings opened from September 2025 to October 2026, the higher-grade postings closed faster. Postings for GS-12 to GS-15 averaged about 7 days from open to close (422 postings, weighted average 7.3 days), while the lower-grade postings (GS-05 to 07 and GS-09, 26 postings) averaged 29.2 days. Some higher-grade postings did run long: a few GS-13 and GS-14 postings stayed open up to 181 to 183 days, so the averages hide a tail. These are posted open-to-close windows, not time to fill; the data has no applicant or hire links, so time to hire is not available. I read this as the posted open window by grade band for all CBP Officer postings in the data; if you meant time to fill, or only postings open on August 1, 2026, say so.

```sql
SELECT minimum_grade, maximum_grade, COUNT(*) AS postings, ROUND(AVG(close_date - open_date), 1) AS avg_days_open, MIN(close_date - open_date) AS min_days_open, MAX(close_date - open_date) AS max_days_open FROM semantic.job_posting WHERE occupational_series_codes ? '1895' AND open_date >= '2025-09-01' AND open_date <= '2026-10-31' GROUP BY minimum_grade, maximum_grade ORDER BY minimum_grade, maximum_grade
```

CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) retired most often in December 2025, with 152 of their 586 retirements in the twelve months from September 2025 to August 2026 (about 26%). question_text: Are higher-graded CBP Officers leaving at a higher rate than lower grades?
answer_text:
Exploratory

No. Across the twelve months to August 2026, the lower grades of CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) left at higher rates than the higher grades. Grades 5 to 9 separated at 0.064 combined, against 0.034 for grades 13 to 15 combined. Grade 12, the largest group, sat at 0.032.

| Grade | Separations | Rate |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | 67 | 0.102 |
| 7 | 81 | 0.077 |
| 9 | 61 | 0.040 |
| 11 | 8 | 0.007 |
| 12 | 550 | 0.032 |
| 13 | 136 | 0.032 |
| 14 | 32 | 0.038 |
| 15 | 12 | 0.066 |

Grade 15 (174 staff at the start) is the one higher grade with a rate above grade 12, and it is a small cell. Grade 0 (36 staff, 0.219) is too small to read. None of the separations in this window carries the 2025 deferred resignation flag, so the rate with and without that wave is the same. Late reports keep arriving, so these counts will rise slightly. Grade headcounts moved a lot over the year (grades 5 to 9 grew from 2,704 to 3,793 while grade 12 fell), so the rates use each grade's average headcount and are approximate. I read "higher-graded" as grades 13 to 15 against the rest, and the rate as the trailing twelve-month rate to August 2026; if you meant the count of separations by grade, say so.

```sql
WITH s AS (SELECT grade, COUNT(*) AS start_hc FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot WHERE snapshot_month = '2025-09-01' AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895' GROUP BY grade), e AS (SELECT grade, COUNT(*) AS end_hc FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01' AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895' GROUP BY grade), sep AS (SELECT grade, COUNT(*) AS seps, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE drp_indicator IS DISTINCT FROM 'Y') AS seps_excl_drp FROM semantic.separation WHERE effective_month BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-01' AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895' GROUP BY grade) SELECT COALESCE(s.grade, e.grade, sep.grade) AS grade, COALESCE(s.start_hc, 0) AS start_hc, COALESCE(e.end_hc, 0) AS end_hc, COALESCE(sep.seps, 0) AS separations, COALESCE(sep.seps_excl_drp, 0) AS separations_excl_drp, ROUND(COALESCE(sep.seps, 0) / NULLIF((COALESCE(s.start_hc, 0) + COALESCE(e.end_hc, 0)) / 2.0, 0), 4) AS rate, ROUND(COALESCE(sep.seps_excl_drp, 0) / NULLIF((COALESCE(s.start_hc, 0) + COALESCE(e.end_hc, 0)) / 2.0, 0), 4) AS rate_excl_drp FROM s FULL OUTER JOIN e ON s.grade = e.grade FULL OUTER JOIN sep ON COALESCE(s.grade, e.grade) = sep.grade ORDER BY grade
```

question_text: Roughly how many CBP Officers could retire in the next five years, going by age bracket and years of service?
answer_text:
Exploratory

About 8,700 CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) could be eligible to retire within five years, as of the August 2026 snapshot: 8,732 of 27,650 officers have 20 or more years of service, and each reaches the law enforcement threshold of 25 years at any age, or age 50 with 20 years, within five years. The age and service brackets cannot show which officers aged 45 and over with 10 to 20 years will reach 20 years within the window, so the true figure lies between 8,732 and about 12,127. Eligibility is not departure, and the count does not apply mandatory separation ages for law enforcement officers.

- 20 years or more, all ages: 28 + 699 + 2,245 + 2,483 + 2,130 + 850 + 297 = 8,732
- Upper bound adds officers aged 45 and over with 10 to 20 years: 1,877 + 900 + 378 + 190 + 50 = 3,395, so 8,732 + 3,395 = 12,127

I read "could retire" as eligibility under those law enforcement retirement rules, counted from the August 2026 snapshot. If you meant actual retirements over the last twelve months, say so.

```sql
SELECT age_bracket,
       CASE WHEN length_of_service_years >= 20 THEN '20+ years'
            WHEN length_of_service_years >= 10 THEN '10 to under 20 years'
            WHEN length_of_service_years >= 5 THEN '5 to under 10 years'
            ELSE 'under 5 years' END AS service_band,
       COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01'
  AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD'
  AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2
```

The OPM data shows 1,041 separations of TSA screeners (Transportation Security Officers, series 1802) effective October and November 2025, 702 of them quits. That is 69 fewer than the 1,110 TSA reported.

October had 541 separations and November had 500. Quits were 372 in October (370 without the deferred resignation flag, 2 with it) and 330 in November. Only 2 quits in the two months came through the 2025 deferred resignation program, so that program does not explain the gap. The records hold separation categories but no reasons, so I cannot say why anyone left. Late reports keep arriving, so these counts will grow slightly. question_text: What's the average salary of TSA screeners, and how does it compare with CBP Officers?
answer_text:
Exploratory
TSA screeners (Transportation Security Administration, 1802) averaged $74,752 in annualized basic pay across 46,913 staff in the August 2026 snapshot, and CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) averaged $104,511 across 27,650 staff. That puts CBP Officers about $29,759 (roughly 40%) above TSA screeners.
The pay figures are estimated: OPM redacted them, so they were filled in from job postings for about 90% of TSA screener rows and all CBP Officer rows. Location figures on both are also estimated, so treat this as a distribution estimate rather than a published average.
I read "salary" as average annualized basic pay across all staff in the cell, for the latest snapshot (August 2026); if you meant the median, or pay by grade, say so.

```sql
SELECT agency_subelement_code, occupational_series_code, COUNT(*) AS headcount, ROUND(CAST(AVG(annualized_adjusted_basic_pay) AS numeric), 0) AS avg_basic_pay, SUM(CASE WHEN pay_imputed THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS pay_imputed_rows, SUM(CASE WHEN location_imputed THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS location_imputed_rows FROM workforce_snapshot WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01' AND ((agency_subelement_code = 'HSBC' AND occupational_series_code = '1802') OR (agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895')) GROUP BY agency_subelement_code, occupational_series_code ORDER BY agency_subelement_code
```

question_text: Which cities have the most CBP Officers?

As of the August 2026 snapshot, CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) totalled 27,650 people. The largest duty-station cities were Washington, District of Columbia (1,956), Sterling, Virginia (790), Ashburn, Virginia (645), El Paso, Texas (540), and Detroit, Michigan (436). Every city figure is estimated. OPM redacted the location for all of these rows, so the city and state were filled in from USAJOBS postings, which show where CBP hires rather than where officers sit. The masking test covers only FEMA and CISA, and it found the state match was 0.11 for FEMA and 0.28 for CISA. CBP was not tested, and the test flatters the method for CBP because its officers spread across many ports of entry, so treat the city ranking as a rough distribution.

question_text: Do higher-grade CBP Officer postings stay open longer than lower-grade ones?
answer_text:
Exploratory
No. Lower-grade CBP Officer postings stayed open longer. Postings with a minimum grade of 5 averaged 29.3 days and grade 9 averaged 22.4 days, while grades 12 to 15 averaged 6.4 to 7.7 days, with a median of 6 days each.

| Minimum grade | Postings | Average days posted | Median days posted |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 14 | 29.3 | 30 |
| 9 | 22 | 22.4 | 28 |
| 12 | 57 | 7.7 | 6 |
| 13 | 211 | 7.4 | 6 |
| 14 | 127 | 7.2 | 6 |
| 15 | 32 | 6.4 | 6 |

These are the announced open-to-close windows for 470 CBP Officer announcements opened September 2025 to October 2026. The records do not show when a posting was filled or cancelled early, and they hold no applicant data, so the windows cannot tell us whether a grade was harder to fill. I read "stay open longer" as the announced posting window by minimum grade; if you meant how many postings were open on a given date, or the maximum grade, say so.

```sql
SELECT minimum_grade, COUNT(*) AS postings, ROUND(AVG(close_date - open_date), 1) AS avg_days_posted, percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY close_date - open_date) AS median_days_posted, MIN(close_date - open_date) AS min_days_posted, MAX(close_date - open_date) AS max_days_posted FROM semantic.job_posting WHERE occupational_series_codes ? '1895' AND open_date BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-10-31' GROUP BY minimum_grade ORDER BY minimum_grade
```

question_text: When in the year do CBP Officers retire? Show retirements by month.

CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) retired 586 times over the twelve months from September 2025 to August 2026, and December is the peak month: 152 of those, about 26% of the year's total. Outside December, monthly retirements ran between 24 and 54 in the fall and 26 to 52 from January to August. None of the retirements carried the deferred resignation program flag, so the December spike is not a program wave. Late reports keep arriving, so the August 2026 count of 31 will likely grow. I read "retire" as all three OPM retirement categories (voluntary, early out, and other) by the month the separation took effect, over the twelve months to August 2026; if you meant a different window, or the separation rate instead, say so.

question_text: Are higher-graded CBP Officers leaving at a higher rate than lower grades?
answer_text:
Exploratory

No. Across the twelve months to August 2026, CBP Officers in the lower grades separated at higher rates than those in the higher grades. Grades 05 and 07 separated at about 0.10 and 0.08, while grades 12 to 14 sat between 0.03 and 0.04. Grade 15 is higher at 0.066, but it rests on about 180 people and 12 separations, so treat it as noisy. The cell as a whole is 0.0351, and no separations in this cell came through the 2025 deferred resignation program, so the rate is the same with and without it.

| Grade | Headcount Sep 2025 | Headcount Aug 2026 | Separations | Rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 00 | 36 | 28 | 7 | 0.219 |
| 05 | 412 | 898 | 67 | 0.102 |
| 07 | 863 | 1,234 | 81 | 0.077 |
| 09 | 1,429 | 1,661 | 61 | 0.039 |
| 11 | 1,125 | 1,270 | 8 | 0.007 |
| 12 | 17,520 | 17,130 | 550 | 0.032 |
| 13 | 4,251 | 4,375 | 136 | 0.032 |
| 14 | 834 | 866 | 32 | 0.038 |
| 15 | 174 | 188 | 12 | 0.066 |

Each rate is separations divided by the average of the September 2025 and August 2026 headcounts (for grade 05: 67 ÷ ((412 + 898) ÷ 2) = 67 ÷ 655 = 0.102). The grade rows sum to the cell total of 954 separations. Late reports keep arriving, so the counts will rise slightly. I read this as the trailing twelve-month separation rate by grade for CBP Officers, all separation types, to August 2026; if you meant the count of separations, or a different window, say so.

```sql
WITH hc_end AS (
  SELECT grade, count(*) AS headcount_end
  FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
  WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01' AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
  GROUP BY grade
),
hc_start AS (
  SELECT grade, count(*) AS headcount_start
  FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
  WHERE snapshot_month = '2025-09-01' AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
  GROUP BY grade
),
sep AS (
  SELECT grade,
         count(*) AS separations,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE drp_indicator IS DISTINCT FROM 'Y') AS separations_excl_drp
  FROM semantic.separation
  WHERE effective_month BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-01'
    AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
  GROUP BY grade
)
SELECT COALESCE(hc_end.grade, hc_start.grade, sep.grade) AS grade,
       hc_start.headcount_start,
       hc_end.headcount_end,
       sep.separations,
       sep.separations_excl_drp
FROM hc_end
FULL JOIN hc_start ON hc_end.grade = hc_start.grade
FULL JOIN sep ON COALESCE(hc_end.grade, hc_start.grade) = sep.grade
ORDER BY 1
```

The analyst supplies this fact, which the data does not contain: The government was shut down from October 1 to November 12, 2025.

Redo that with the shutdown taken out.
turn_1_answer_text:
Verified
CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) landed 475 accessions against a plan of 594 hires in FY2026 Q1 (October to December 2025), a variance of -119 hires, or -20.0% of plan. Later OPM files add accessions as late records arrive, so this gap will narrow. I read "hiring" as accessions against planned hires for CBP Officers in that quarter; if you meant separations or monthly accession counts, say so.
answer_text:
Verified
Assuming, as you state, that no one could be onboarded from October 1 to November 12, 2025, the scaled plan for CBP Officers in FY2026 Q1 (October to December 2025) is about 316 hires, and the 475 actual accessions land about 159 hires (+50.1%) above it. Against the full plan of 594, the variance was -119 hires (-20.0%). This shows what the comparison looks like under your assumption; it does not show that the shutdown caused the result.

- Days in the quarter: October 1 to December 31, 2025 = 31 + 30 + 31 = 92
- Days hiring could not happen: October 1 to November 12 = 31 + 12 = 43
- Days hiring was possible: 92 - 43 = 49
- Scaled plan: 594 × 49 / 92 = 316.4 hires
- Variance against the scaled plan: 475 - 316.4 = +158.6 hires, or 158.6 / 316.4 = +50.1%

Later OPM files can still add accessions. Accessions by month for October to December 2025 are the better test of your assumption, since any onboarding in October or early November would contradict it. I read this as prorating the plan by days; if you want a different treatment of the blocked days, say so.

question_text: TSA told Congress about 1,110 screeners left during the October and November 2025 shutdown. What does the OPM data show, and how many of those were quits?
answer_text:
Exploratory

The OPM data shows 1,041 TSA screener (1802) separations with effective dates in October and November 2025: 541 in October and 500 in November. Of those, 702 were quits (372 in October, 330 in November), about 67 percent of the total. That is 69 fewer separations than the 1,110 TSA reported to Congress. The data does not show what TSA counted, so I cannot say whether the gap is scope or timing. These months are old enough that late reports should be mostly in, though about 0.8 percent of records are later restated. The data records separation categories, not reasons, so it cannot show why anyone quit or whether the shutdown caused it.

```sql
SELECT effective_month, separation_category, drp_indicator, COUNT(*) AS separations
FROM semantic.separation
WHERE agency_subelement_code = 'HSBC'
  AND occupational_series_code = '1802'
  AND effective_month BETWEEN '2025-10-01' AND '2025-11-01'
GROUP BY effective_month, separation_category, drp_indicator
ORDER BY effective_month, separation_category, drp_indicator
```

I read this as all separations of TSA screeners effective October and November 2025, counted from the OPM monthly files. If you meant all TSA occupations, or the separation rate instead of the count, say so.

question_text: What's the average salary of TSA screeners, and how does it compare with CBP Officers?
answer_text:
Exploratory

As of the August 2026 snapshot, CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) average $104,511 in annualized basic pay, against $74,752 for TSA screeners (Transportation Security Administration, 1802). That is a gap of $29,759, or about 40% more for CBP Officers ($29,759 ÷ $74,752 = 39.8%).

Both averages are estimated. OPM redacted pay for 42,225 of the 46,913 TSA screeners (90%) and for all 27,650 CBP Officers, so those figures were filled in from job postings. I read "average salary" as the mean annualized basic pay per employee at the latest snapshot; if you meant median pay, total compensation, or another month, say so.

```sql
SELECT agency_subelement_code, occupational_series_code, COUNT(*) AS headcount, ROUND(AVG(annualized_adjusted_basic_pay)::numeric, 0) AS avg_basic_pay, SUM(CASE WHEN pay_imputed THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS pay_imputed_rows FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01' AND ((agency_subelement_code = 'HSBC' AND occupational_series_code = '1802') OR (agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895')) GROUP BY agency_subelement_code, occupational_series_code ORDER BY agency_subelement_code
```

question_text: Which cities have the most CBP Officers?
answer_text:
Exploratory

Washington, District of Columbia has the most CBP Officers by duty station city in the August 2026 snapshot, with 1,956 officers, followed by Sterling and Ashburn in Virginia. Every city figure is estimated: OPM redacted these locations, so they were filled in from USAJOBS postings, which show where CBP hires rather than where officers sit. The masking test was run only on FEMA and CISA. Their drawn state matched the true state 11% and 28% of the time, with distribution overlap of 0.66 and 0.78. That test flatters the method for CBP, whose officers are spread across hundreds of airports and ports, so treat this ranking as directional, not a head count by city.

| 6 | Houston, Texas | 392 |

question_text: How many postings listed the Border Patrol series 1896 between September 2025 and October 2026, counting ones that list several series?
answer_text:
Exploratory

889 USAJOBS postings listed Border Patrol Agent (series 1896) in the window, counting postings that list several series. The window is announcements opened from September 1, 2025 to October 31, 2026, across all of DHS. Each posting is counted once, and it counts if 1896 appears anywhere in its list of series.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT control_number) AS postings_listing_1896, COUNT(*) AS rows_counted FROM semantic.job_posting WHERE open_date >= DATE '2025-09-01' AND open_date <= DATE '2026-10-31' AND occupational_series_codes ? '1896'
```

question_text: Do higher-grade CBP Officer postings stay open longer than lower-grade ones?
answer_text:
Exploratory

No. In the postings that list the CBP Officer series (1895) and opened from September 2025 to October 2026, higher-grade announcements closed sooner, not later. Grade 15 postings averaged 6.4 days open, grades 12 to 14 about 7 to 8 days, and grade 5 to 7 and grade 9 postings averaged 29.2 days each. The query covered 470 postings and filtered on the series, not the component, so a few may be from outside CBP.

| Grade (min to max) | Postings | Average days open |
|---|---|---|
| 5 to 7 | 13 | 29.2 |
| 9 | 13 | 29.2 |
| 12 | 55 | 7.7 |
| 13 | 208 | 7.3 |
| 14 | 127 | 7.2 |
| 15 | 32 | 6.4 |

These are advertised windows (open date to close date), not time to fill. Postings filled or cancelled early are not visible, and nothing links a posting to the people hired through it, so the data cannot show whether long-open postings fill more slowly. Averages include some long outliers, such as one grade 14 posting open 183 days. I read "stay open longer" as the advertised window by grade; if you meant time to fill or the count of hires per posting, the records do not hold that, and the nearest available measure is accessions by month.

```sql
SELECT minimum_grade, maximum_grade, COUNT(*) AS postings, ROUND(AVG(close_date - open_date), 1) AS avg_days_open, MIN(close_date - open_date) AS min_days_open, MAX(close_date - open_date) AS max_days_open FROM semantic.job_posting WHERE occupational_series_codes ? '1895' AND open_date >= '2025-09-01' AND open_date <= '2026-10-31' GROUP BY minimum_grade, maximum_grade ORDER BY minimum_grade, maximum_grade
```

question_text: When in the year do CBP Officers retire? Show retirements by month.

CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) retirements peak in December: 152 of the 586 retirements in the twelve months from September 2025 to August 2026 fell in December 2025, about 26%. Every other month ran between 24 and 54, with no deferred resignation program retirements in any month. Late reports keep arriving, so the most recent months, especially August 2026, will grow.

|---|---|
| 2025-09 | 54 |
| 2025-10 | 36 |
| 2025-11 | 24 |
| 2025-12 | 152 |
| 2026-01 | 44 |
| 2026-02 | 26 |
| 2026-03 | 31 |
| 2026-04 | 45 |
| 2026-05 | 52 |
| 2026-06 | 46 |
| 2026-07 | 45 |
| 2026-08 | 31 |

I read this as all three retirement categories (voluntary, early out, and other) for CBP Officers, by effective month, over September 2025 to August 2026; if you meant only voluntary retirements or a different twelve months, say so.

question_text: How many CBP Officers who left this year had less than one year of service?
answer_text:
Exploratory

CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) with less than one year of service made 170 separations in the twelve months the data covers, September 2025 to August 2026. Of those, 138 fell in calendar 2026 (January to August) and 32 in September to December 2025. None came through the 2025 deferred resignation program. Late reports keep arriving, so these counts will grow slightly.

I read "this year" as the twelve months the data covers, September 2025 to August 2026, and I counted every separation category. If you meant only calendar 2026, the figure is 138; if you meant the separation rate, say so.

```sql
SELECT CASE WHEN s.effective_month >= '2026-01-01' THEN 'calendar 2026 (Jan to Aug 2026)' ELSE 'Sep 2025 to Aug 2026' END AS period, COUNT(*) AS separations_under_1_year, SUM(CASE WHEN s.drp_indicator = 'Y' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS drp_separations FROM semantic.separation s WHERE s.agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND s.occupational_series_code = '1895' AND s.effective_month BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-01' AND s.length_of_service_years < 1 GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
```

question_text: Which DHS components lost the most senior executives this year?
answer_text:
Exploratory

Over the trailing twelve months (September 2025 to August 2026), DHS Headquarters lost the most senior executives (57 separations), followed by FEMA (44), ICE (37), CBP (31), USCIS (30), CISA (27) and the Secret Service (23). TSA recorded none. Of the 273 senior executive separations DHS-wide, 62 came through the 2025 deferred resignation program, and 116 fell in January to August 2026. Late reports keep arriving, so recent counts will grow. These are counts, not rates; I have not divided by senior executive headcount, so large components will look bigger.

| Component | Trailing 12 months | Excluding deferred resignation | January to August 2026 |
|---|---|---|---|
| DHS Headquarters (HSAA) | 57 | 42 | 29 |
| FEMA (HSCB) | 44 | 21 | 18 |
| ICE (HSBB) | 37 | 37 | 21 |
| CBP (HSBD) | 31 | 31 | 18 |
| USCIS (HSAB) | 30 | 21 | 6 |
| CISA (HSCA) | 27 | 20 | 4 |
| Secret Service (HSAD) | 23 | 23 | 11 |

The table omits five components with fewer than ten separations in total: S&T (8), Coast Guard (7), FLETC (4), DNDO (3, not one of the twelve codes) and OIG (2). I read "this year" as the trailing twelve months to August 2026 and "senior executives" as the Senior Executive Service pay plan, counted by separations. If you meant the separation rate against senior executive headcount, or calendar 2026 only, say so.

```sql
SELECT agency_subelement_code, agency_subelement, COUNT(*) AS separations_trailing_12m, SUM(CASE WHEN drp_indicator = 'Y' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS drp_separations, SUM(CASE WHEN drp_indicator = 'Y' THEN 0 ELSE 1 END) AS separations_excl_drp, SUM(CASE WHEN effective_month BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-08-01' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS separations_calendar_2026_to_aug FROM semantic.separation WHERE pay_plan_code = 'ES' AND effective_month BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-01' GROUP BY agency_subelement_code, agency_subelement ORDER BY separations_trailing_12m DESC
```

question_text: Are higher-graded CBP Officers leaving at a higher rate than lower grades?
answer_text:
Exploratory

No. For CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895), the trailing twelve-month separation rate to August 2026 falls as grade rises from 5 to 13. Grades 5 and 7 leave at about 0.10 and 0.08, grades 12 and 13 at about 0.03, and grade 15 reads 0.066 on only 181 officers and 12 separations.

| Grade | Mean headcount | Separations | Rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 655 | 67 | 0.1023 |
| 7 | 1,049 | 81 | 0.0773 |
| 9 | 1,545 | 61 | 0.0395 |
| 12 | 17,325 | 550 | 0.0317 |
| 13 | 4,313 | 136 | 0.0315 |
| 14 | 850 | 32 | 0.0376 |
| 15 | 181 | 12 | 0.0663 |

Every separation for these officers is outside the 2025 deferred resignation program, so the rate is the same with and without it. Late reports keep arriving, so the counts will grow. Grades 5 and 7 grew sharply over the year, so their mean-headcount denominators are rough. Grades 0 and 11 are also excluded from the table because they are too small or too sparse to read.

I read this as the trailing twelve-month separation rate by grade to August 2026; if you meant separation counts, or a different period, say so.

```sql
SELECT g.grade, g.start_hc, g.end_hc, COALESCE(s.sep_total, 0) AS sep_total, COALESCE(s.sep_excl_drp, 0) AS sep_excl_drp
FROM (
  SELECT grade,
         COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE snapshot_month = '2025-09-01') AS start_hc,
         COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01') AS end_hc
  FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
  WHERE agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD'
    AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
    AND snapshot_month IN ('2025-09-01', '2026-08-01')
  GROUP BY grade
) g
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT grade,
         COUNT(*) AS sep_total,
         COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE drp_indicator IS DISTINCT FROM 'Y') AS sep_excl_drp
  FROM semantic.separation
  WHERE agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD'
    AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
    AND effective_month BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-01'
  GROUP BY grade
) s ON s.grade = g.grade
ORDER BY g.grade
```

question_text: Roughly how many CBP Officers could retire in the next five years, going by age bracket and years of service?
answer_text:
Exploratory

About 11,400 of the 27,650 CBP Officers on the August 2026 snapshot (41%) would be eligible to retire at some point by August 2031, and about 6,200 of them are already eligible. Eligibility is not the same as leaving, so treat this as a ceiling on who could go, not a forecast.

| Age bracket | Eligible within five years |
|---|---|
| Under 45 (20+ years of service) | 727 |
| 45-49 | 3,575 |
| 50-54 | 3,250 |
| 55-59 | 2,463 |
| 60-64 | 1,026 |
| 65 or more | 346 |

The eligibility rule is my assumption, not something the snapshot states: age 50 with 20 years of service, or 25 years at any age, applied to the bracketed ages and the service years in the records. I used the latest snapshot (August 2026) for the headcount, not the FY2026 Q1 cell. I read "could retire" as eligibility on that headcount; if you meant the number who will actually leave, the separation rate for these officers is the nearest measure.

Two one-off queries produced these numbers. The first gave headcount by age bracket and service band:

```sql
SELECT age_bracket,
  CASE WHEN length_of_service_years < 1 THEN '<1'
       WHEN length_of_service_years < 3 THEN '1-3'
       WHEN length_of_service_years < 5 THEN '3-5'
       WHEN length_of_service_years < 10 THEN '5-10'
       WHEN length_of_service_years < 20 THEN '10-20'
       ELSE '20+' END AS service_bucket,
  COUNT(*) AS headcount,
  SUM(CASE WHEN location_imputed THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS location_imputed_rows
FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01'
  AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD'
  AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2
```

The second split officers with 10+ years of service into single years, so the 15-year and 20-year thresholds could be applied:

```sql
SELECT age_bracket,
  FLOOR(length_of_service_years)::int AS service_years,
  COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01'
  AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD'
  AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
  AND length_of_service_years >= 10
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2
```

- Days in the quarter: October 1 to December 31, 2025 = 31 + 30 + 31 = 92
- Days hiring could not happen: October 1 to November 12 = 31 + 12 = 43
- Days hiring was possible: 92 - 43 = 49
- Scaled plan: 594 x 49 / 92 = 316.4
- Variance against the scaled plan: 475 - 316.4 = +158.6, or 158.6 / 316.4 = +50.1%

question_text: Which cities have the most CBP Officers?
answer_text:
Exploratory
Washington, District of Columbia (1,956), Sterling, Virginia (790), and Ashburn, Virginia (645) have the most CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, series 1895) as of the August 2026 snapshot. Those top 25 cities hold 10,275 of the 27,650 officers, about 37%. Every CBP row carries an estimated location, filled in from job postings rather than published by OPM, so these city counts show where CBP posts its hiring, not where officers sit. The only masking test I could retrieve covers FEMA and CISA (state match 11% and 28%), and it flatters the method for CBP, so the CBP city figures are less reliable than those numbers suggest. Late OPM files may still adjust these counts.

```sql
WITH base AS (
  SELECT duty_station_city, duty_station_state,
         COUNT(*) AS headcount,
         SUM(CASE WHEN location_imputed THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS imputed_rows
  FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
  WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01'
    AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD'
    AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
  GROUP BY duty_station_city, duty_station_state
)
SELECT duty_station_city, duty_station_state, headcount, imputed_rows,
       SUM(headcount) OVER () AS total_headcount,
       SUM(imputed_rows) OVER () AS total_imputed_rows
FROM base
ORDER BY headcount DESC
LIMIT 25
```

question_text: Are higher-graded CBP Officers leaving at a higher rate than lower grades?
answer_text:
Exploratory

No, not as a group: CBP Officers in grades 05 to 09 separated at about 6.4% over the twelve months to August 2026, while grades 13 to 15 separated at about 3.4%, and grade 12 at 3.2%. Grade 15 is the exception at 6.6%, but that rests on 12 separations against about 181 average staff.

The rates use the headcount at September 2025 and August 2026 as the mean base. Grades 05 to 09 pooled: 209 separations ÷ ((2,704 + 3,793) ÷ 2 = 3,248.5) = 0.064. Grades 13 to 15 pooled: 180 ÷ ((5,259 + 5,429) ÷ 2 = 5,344) = 0.034. The one-off query found no deferred resignation program flags among these officers' separations in the window, so the rate is the same with and without that wave. Late reports keep arriving, so recent separations will grow, and grade 05 and grade 12 headcounts moved a lot between the two snapshots.

| Grade | Average staff | Separations | Rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| 05 | 655 | 67 | 0.102 |
| 07 | 1,049 | 81 | 0.077 |
| 09 | 1,545 | 61 | 0.039 |
| 11 | 1,198 | 8 | 0.007 |
| 12 | 17,325 | 550 | 0.032 |
| 13 | 4,313 | 136 | 0.032 |
| 14 | 850 | 32 | 0.038 |
| 15 | 181 | 12 | 0.066 |

I read "higher-graded" as grades 13 to 15 against grades 05 to 09, with grade 12 shown separately because it holds about two-thirds of the officers; if you meant a pay band or separation counts, say so.

```sql
WITH hc AS (
  SELECT grade,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE snapshot_month = '2025-09-01') AS hc_start,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01') AS hc_end
  FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
  WHERE agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
    AND snapshot_month IN ('2025-09-01', '2026-08-01')
  GROUP BY grade
),
sp AS (
  SELECT grade,
    count(*) AS separations,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE drp_indicator IS DISTINCT FROM 'Y') AS separations_excl_drp
  FROM semantic.separation
  WHERE agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
    AND effective_month BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-01'
  GROUP BY grade
)
SELECT COALESCE(hc.grade, sp.grade) AS grade,
  hc.hc_start, hc.hc_end, sp.separations, sp.separations_excl_drp,
  sp.separations / NULLIF((hc.hc_start + hc.hc_end) / 2.0, 0) AS rate,
  sp.separations_excl_drp / NULLIF((hc.hc_start + hc.hc_end) / 2.0, 0) AS rate_excl_drp
FROM hc
FULL OUTER JOIN sp ON hc.grade = sp.grade
ORDER BY grade
```

question_text: Roughly how many CBP Officers could retire in the next five years, going by age bracket and years of service?
answer_text:
Exploratory

About 11,390 CBP Officers (roughly 41% of the 27,650 on the August 2026 snapshot) could be retirement-eligible by August 2031: 6,193 already are, and 5,194 more would become eligible within five years. Eligibility is a ceiling, not a forecast of departures, and the count does not model mandatory retirement ages.

I read "could retire" as federal law-enforcement retirement eligibility (age 50 with 20 years of service, or 25 years at any age). That rule is my assumption, not something the records hold, so confirm it with the retirement office. If you meant the expected number of retirements, say so. The 27,650 total is the sum of the age-bracket rows from the first query.

Already eligible: 50 and over with 20+ years (2,483 + 2,130 + 850 + 297 = 5,760), plus under 50 with 25+ years (26 + 407 = 433), for 6,193.
Becoming eligible within five years: 45–49 with 20–24 years (1,838), 45–49 with 15–19 years (1,330), 40–44 with 20–24 years (673), 35–39 with 20–24 years (28), and 50–65+ with 15–19 years (767 + 333 + 176 + 49 = 1,325), for 5,194.
Total: 6,193 + 5,194 = 11,387.

```sql
SELECT age_bracket, COUNT(*) AS headcount, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE length_of_service_years >= 20) AS served_20_plus, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE length_of_service_years >= 25) AS served_25_plus, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE length_of_service_years < 20) AS served_under_20 FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01' AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895' GROUP BY age_bracket ORDER BY age_bracket
```

Assuming, as you state, that no one could be onboarded from October 1 to November 12, 2025, the plan scaled to the days hiring was possible is about 316 hires. Against that scaled plan, the 475 actual accessions land +159 (+50.1%), compared with -119 (-20.0%) against the full plan of 594 for CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) in FY2026 Q1 (October to December 2025).

- Days in the quarter: October 1 to December 31, 2025 = 31 + 30 + 31 = 92
- Days hiring could not happen: October 1 to November 12 = 31 + 12 = 43
- Days hiring was possible: 92 - 43 = 49
- Scaled plan: 594 x 49 / 92 = 316.4
- Variance against the scaled plan: 475 - 316.4 = +158.6, or 158.6 / 316.4 = +50.1%

This comparison does not show that the assumption explains the shortfall. The 475 accessions are recorded across the quarter, so they suggest some onboarding did occur before November 12. Accessions by month for October to December 2025 would test the assumption directly, and a one-off query can produce them. Later OPM files may also add accessions. question_text: TSA told Congress about 1,110 screeners left during the October and November 2025 shutdown. What does the OPM data show, and how many of those were quits?
answer_text:
Exploratory

The OPM data shows 1,041 TSA screener (1802) separations effective October and November 2025, of which 702 were quits (370 plus 2 in October, 330 in November). That is 67% of all separations in those two months.

Counts by month: October had 541 separations (372 quits) and November had 500 (330 quits). Four of the October quits and retirements came through the 2025 deferred resignation program; November shows none. The OPM total is 69 below TSA's 1,110. I can't tell from the data what TSA counted, so I'd check its scope before quoting either figure. Late reports keep arriving, but these months are old enough that the count should be close to settled.

I read "screeners" as TSA's Compliance Inspection and Support series (1802), "left" as all separation categories, and "quits" as the QUIT category, with and without the deferred resignation flag. If TSA's 1,110 covers all TSA occupations rather than screeners alone, I can run that comparison.

```sql
SELECT effective_month, separation_category, drp_indicator, COUNT(*) AS separations
FROM semantic.separation
WHERE effective_month BETWEEN '2025-10-01' AND '2025-11-01'
  AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBC'
  AND occupational_series_code = '1802'
GROUP BY effective_month, separation_category, drp_indicator
ORDER BY effective_month, separation_category, drp_indicator
```

question_text: What's the average salary of TSA screeners, and how does it compare with CBP Officers?
answer_text:
Exploratory

TSA screeners (Compliance Inspection and Support, 1802) averaged about $74,752 in annualized basic pay as of the August 2026 snapshot, against about $104,511 for CBP Officers (1895). That is roughly $29,759 (about 40%) more for CBP Officers. Both averages are estimated: 42,225 of the 46,913 TSA screener rows (90%) and all 27,650 CBP Officer rows have pay estimated from job postings, not published by OPM.

I read this as average basic pay for all staff in each series at the August 2026 snapshot; if you meant the pay band or grade mix, or a different month, say so.

question_text: Which cities have the most CBP Officers?

question_text: Do higher-grade CBP Officer postings stay open longer than lower-grade ones?
answer_text:
Exploratory
No. Higher-grade CBP Officer postings close sooner, not later: the GS-13 to GS-15 postings averaged 7.3 days open, against 8.3 days for GS-11 to GS-12 and about 29 days for GS-07 and GS-09 (postings opened September 2025 to October 2026, 470 in total).

Medians tell the same story: 6 days for GS-11 to GS-15 and 30 days for the lower grades. The lower-grade group is only 27 postings, and a few GS-13 and GS-14 postings stayed open up to about 180 days, so treat the averages as indicative. The six postings with no GS grade (grade 00) averaged 13.3 days and are left out of the comparison.

I read "open longer" as the announced window (close date minus open date) for postings that list series 1895, grouped by maximum grade. The nearest alternative is time to fill, which the records cannot answer, because postings are not linked to the people hired through them.

```sql
SELECT minimum_grade, maximum_grade, COUNT(*) AS postings, ROUND(AVG(close_date - open_date), 1) AS avg_days_open, MIN(close_date - open_date) AS min_days_open, MAX(close_date - open_date) AS max_days_open FROM semantic.job_posting WHERE occupational_series_codes ? '1895' AND open_date >= '2025-09-01' AND open_date <= '2026-10-31' GROUP BY minimum_grade, maximum_grade ORDER BY maximum_grade, minimum_grade
```
