question_text: When in the year do CBP Officers retire? Show retirements by month.
answer_text:
Exploratory

CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) retired 586 times in the twelve effective months from September 2025 to August 2026, and December 2025 is the peak month with 152, about 26% of the total. Excluding December, the other eleven months average about 39 retirements (434 ÷ 11 = 39.5). None of these retirements came through the 2025 deferred resignation program. Late reports keep arriving, so the most recent months (July and August 2026) will grow.

I read "retire" as all three retirement categories (voluntary, early out, and other) and "the year" as the twelve effective months to August 2026. If you meant calendar 2026 only, or want the split by retirement category, say so.

SELECT to_char(effective_month, 'YYYY-MM') AS month, COUNT(*) AS retirements, SUM(CASE WHEN drp_indicator = 'Y' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS drp_retirements FROM semantic.separation WHERE agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895' AND effective_month BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-01' AND separation_category LIKE 'RETIREMENT%' GROUP BY effective_month ORDER BY effective_month

question_text: Are higher-graded CBP Officers leaving at a higher rate than lower grades?
answer_text:
Exploratory

No. Across the twelve months to August 2026, CBP Officers at GS-13 and above separated at about the same rate as GS-12 staff (0.0317), and the highest rate is at GS-15 (0.0663) on only 12 separations. The lowest grades left fastest (GS-05 at 0.1023, GS-07 at 0.0773). The cell as a whole separated at 0.0351 (954 separations on an average headcount of 27,147).

| Grade | Headcount Sep 2025 | Headcount Aug 2026 | Separations | Rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GS-05 | 412 | 898 | 67 | 0.1023 |
| GS-07 | 863 | 1,234 | 81 | 0.0773 |
| GS-09 | 1,429 | 1,661 | 61 | 0.0395 |
| GS-11 | 1,125 | 1,270 | 8 | 0.0067 |
| GS-12 | 17,520 | 17,130 | 550 | 0.0317 |
| GS-13 | 4,251 | 4,375 | 136 | 0.0315 |
| GS-14 | 834 | 866 | 32 | 0.0376 |
| GS-15 | 174 | 188 | 12 | 0.0663 |
| ES (Senior Executive) | 36 | 28 | 7 | 0.2188 |

No separations in this cell carry the 2025 deferred resignation flag, so the rates with and without that wave are the same. Late reports keep arriving, so these rates will rise slightly. The GS-15 and Senior Executive rows rest on small groups, so a single departure moves them by several points. I read "higher-graded" as GS-13 and above, with the Senior Executive grade shown separately; if you meant the rate by pay band or the count of separations, say so.

```sql
WITH hs AS (
  SELECT pay_plan_code, grade, COUNT(*) AS hc_start
  FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
  WHERE agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895' AND snapshot_month = '2025-09-01'
  GROUP BY pay_plan_code, grade
),
he AS (
  SELECT pay_plan_code, grade, COUNT(*) AS hc_end
  FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
  WHERE agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895' AND snapshot_month = '2026-08-01'
  GROUP BY pay_plan_code, grade
),
sp AS (
  SELECT pay_plan_code, grade, COUNT(*) AS seps_all,
         COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE drp_indicator IS DISTINCT FROM 'Y') AS seps_excl_drp
  FROM semantic.separation
  WHERE agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
    AND effective_month BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-01'
  GROUP BY pay_plan_code, grade
)
SELECT COALESCE(hs.pay_plan_code, he.pay_plan_code, sp.pay_plan_code) AS pay_plan_code,
       COALESCE(hs.grade, he.grade, sp.grade) AS grade,
       COALESCE(hs.hc_start, 0) AS hc_start,
       COALESCE(he.hc_end, 0) AS hc_end,
       COALESCE(sp.seps_all, 0) AS seps_all,
       COALESCE(sp.seps_excl_drp, 0) AS seps_excl_drp,
       ROUND(COALESCE(sp.seps_all,0)::numeric / NULLIF((COALESCE(hs.hc_start,0)+COALESCE(he.hc_end,0))/2.0, 0), 4) AS rate,
       ROUND(COALESCE(sp.seps_excl_drp,0)::numeric / NULLIF((COALESCE(hs.hc_start,0)+COALESCE(he.hc_end,0))/2.0, 0), 4) AS rate_excl_drp
FROM hs
FULL OUTER JOIN he ON he.pay_plan_code = hs.pay_plan_code AND he.grade = hs.grade
FULL OUTER JOIN sp ON sp.pay_plan_code = COALESCE(hs.pay_plan_code, he.pay_plan_code) AND sp.grade = COALESCE(hs.grade, he.grade)
ORDER BY pay_plan_code, grade
```

    AND effective_month BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-01'
  GROUP BY pay_plan_code, grade
)
SELECT COALESCE(hs.pay_plan_code, he.pay_plan_code, sp.pay_plan_code) AS pay_plan_code,
       COALESCE(hs.grade, he.grade, sp.grade) AS grade,
       COALESCE(hs.hc_start, 0) AS hc_start,
       COALESCE(he.hc_end, 0) AS hc_end,
       COALESCE(sp.seps_all, 0) AS seps_all,
       COALESCE(sp.seps_excl_drp, 0) AS seps_excl_drp,
       ROUND(COALESCE(sp.seps_all,0)::numeric / NULLIF((COALESCE(hs.hc_start,0)+COALESCE(he.hc_end,0))/2.0, 0), 4) AS rate,
       ROUND(COALESCE(sp.seps_excl_drp,0)::numeric / NULLIF((COALESCE(hs.hc_start,0)+COALESCE(he.hc_end,0))/2.0, 0), 4) AS rate_excl_drp
FROM hs
FULL OUTER JOIN he ON he.pay_plan_code = hs.pay_plan_code AND he.grade = hs.grade
FULL OUTER JOIN sp ON sp.pay_plan_code = COALESCE(hs.pay_plan_code, he.pay_plan_code) AND sp.grade = COALESCE(hs.grade, he.grade)
ORDER BY pay_plan_code, grade

answer_text:
Verified
Assuming, as you state, that no one could be onboarded from October 1 to November 12, 2025, the plan scaled to the days hiring was possible is about 316 hires. The 475 actual accessions land 159 hires (50.1%) above that scaled plan, compared with 119 hires (20.0%) below the full plan of 594. The scaled comparison is only as good as the assumption. Accessions are counted by effective month, so if any of the 475 took effect between October 1 and November 12, the data does not fit the assumption.

- Days in the quarter: October 1 to December 31, 2025 = 31 + 30 + 31 = 92
- Days hiring could not happen: October 1 to November 12 = 31 + 12 = 43
- Days hiring was possible: 92 - 43 = 49
- Scaled plan: 594 x 49 / 92 = 316.4
- Variance against the scaled plan: 475 - 316.4 = +158.6, or 158.6 / 316.4 = 50.1%

Later OPM files can add accessions. Accessions by month for October to December 2025 would test the assumption directly; a one-off query can pull them. I read this as the FY2026 Q1 plan variance for CBP Officers with the shutdown days removed; if you meant a different quarter or a different measure, say so.

Exploratory

889 postings listed Border Patrol Agent (series 1896) with an open date between September 1, 2025 and October 31, 2026. Each of the 889 is a distinct announcement, and none of the 1896 postings lists more than one series, so counting multi-series postings changes nothing here. Across all DHS postings in that window, 133 do list several series, but none of them include 1896.

I read this as postings opened in the window that list 1896 anywhere in their series list; if you meant postings open on a single date, or only postings where 1896 is the first-listed series, say so.

'1896' AND open_date >= '2025-09-01' AND open_date <= '2026-10-31'

question_text: Do higher-grade CBP Officer postings stay open longer than lower-grade ones?
answer_text:
Exploratory

No. In the postings, the higher grades stayed open for less time: grades 7 and 9 averaged about 29 days from open to close, while grades 12 to 15 averaged 6 to 8 days. The posted windows are 470 CBP Officer announcements opened September 2025 to October 2026, grouped by maximum grade.

| Maximum grade | Postings | Average window (days) | Range (days) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | 13 | 29.2 | 25 to 32 |
| 9 | 14 | 29.3 | 25 to 32 |
| 11 | 3 | 8.0 | 6 to 12 |
| 12 | 62 | 8.3 | 4 to 31 |
| 13 | 210 | 7.3 | 4 to 181 |
| 14 | 130 | 7.5 | 4 to 183 |
| 15 | 32 | 6.4 | 4 to 14 |
| 00 | 6 | 13.3 | 13 to 14 |

These are posted windows (close date minus open date), not how long each posting was actually open, because postings filled or cancelled early are invisible. Nothing links a posting to the people hired through it, so this does not measure time to hire. Grades 11 and 00 have too few postings to read. I read this as all CBP Officer (series 1895) postings opened September 2025 to October 2026, compared by maximum grade; if you meant postings open on a given date, or only the CBP component, say so.

```sql
SELECT maximum_grade, COUNT(*) AS postings, ROUND(AVG(close_date - open_date), 1) AS avg_window_days, MIN(close_date - open_date) AS min_window_days, MAX(close_date - open_date) AS max_window_days FROM semantic.job_posting WHERE occupational_series_codes ? '1895' AND open_date BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-10-31' GROUP BY maximum_grade ORDER BY maximum_grade
```

question_text: When in the year do CBP Officers retire? Show retirements by month.
answer_text:
Exploratory

CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) retired most in December, with 152 of 586 retirements (26%) in the twelve months from September 2025 to August 2026. The count is lowest in November (24) and February (26), and the rest of the year runs between 31 and 54 a month.

| Month | Retirements |
|---|---|
| 2025-09 | 54 |
| 2025-10 | 36 |
| 2025-11 | 24 |
| 2025-12 | 152 |
| 2026-01 | 44 |
| 2026-02 | 26 |
| 2026-03 | 31 |
| 2026-04 | 45 |
| 2026-05 | 52 |
| 2026-06 | 46 |
| 2026-07 | 45 |
| 2026-08 | 31 |

None of these retirements came through the 2025 deferred resignation program. Late reports keep arriving, so the most recent months, especially August 2026, will grow.

I read this as all three retirement categories (voluntary, early out, and other) by effective month over September 2025 to August 2026. If you meant only calendar 2026, or only the open quarter (October to December 2025, where the December figure falls), say so.

```sql
SELECT effective_month, COUNT(*) AS retirements, SUM(CASE WHEN drp_indicator = 'Y' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS drp_retirements FROM semantic.separation WHERE agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895' AND separation_category LIKE 'RETIREMENT%' AND effective_month BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-01' GROUP BY effective_month ORDER BY effective_month
```

question_text: How many CBP Officers who left this year had less than one year of service?
answer_text:
Exploratory

I count 170 CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) with under one year of federal service among separations in the twelve months to August 2026 (September 2025 to August 2026). Of those, 138 separated in calendar 2026 (January to August) and 32 in September to December 2025. Those 170 are out of 954 separations in the twelve months. Late reports keep arriving, so this count will grow slightly.

I read "this year" as the twelve months to August 2026, since the question names no year, and gave calendar 2026 second. If you meant calendar 2026 only, the figure is 138.

```sql
SELECT CASE WHEN effective_month >= '2026-01-01' THEN 'CY2026 (Jan to Aug 2026)' ELSE 'Trailing 12 months (Sep 2025 to Aug 2026)' END AS period, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE length_of_service_years < 1) AS under_one_year, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE length_of_service_years >= 1) AS one_year_or_more, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE length_of_service_years IS NULL) AS service_unknown, COUNT(*) AS all_separations FROM separation WHERE agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895' AND effective_month BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-01' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
```

question_text: Which DHS components lost the most senior executives this year?
answer_text:
Exploratory

DHS Headquarters lost the most senior executives over the twelve months from September 2025 to August 2026, with 57 separations. FEMA followed with 44 and ICE with 37, and CBP lost 31.

| Component | Twelve months to Aug 2026 | Of which 2025 DRP wave | Calendar 2026 (Jan to Aug) |
|---|---|---|---|
| DHS Headquarters (HSAA) | 57 | 15 | 29 |
| FEMA (HSCB) | 44 | 23 | 18 |
| ICE (HSBB) | 37 | 0 | 21 |
| CBP (HSBD) | 31 | 0 | 18 |
| USCIS (HSAB) | 30 | 9 | 6 |
| CISA (HSCA) | 27 | 7 | 4 |
| Secret Service (HSAD) | 23 | 0 | 11 |
| S&T (HSFA) | 8 | 5 | 1 |
| Coast Guard (HSAC) | 7 | 1 | 4 |
| FLETC (HSBE) | 4 | 0 | 3 |
| Domestic Nuclear Detection Office (HSDA) | 3 | 1 | 0 |
| Office of the Inspector General (HSAE) | 2 | 1 | 1 |

These are counts, not rates, so a large component will look worse than a small one. Of the 273 separations, 62 came through the 2025 deferred resignation program wave, mostly at FEMA and DHS Headquarters. Late reports keep arriving, so these counts will grow slightly. I read "senior executives" as the Senior Executive Service pay plan and "this year" as the twelve months the data covers; if you meant calendar 2026 only, use the third column, or if you want rates, say so and I will pull the senior executive headcount for each component.

```sql
SELECT agency_subelement_code, agency_subelement, COUNT(*) AS separations_twelve_months, SUM(CASE WHEN drp_indicator = 'Y' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS drp_separations, SUM(CASE WHEN effective_month >= '2026-01-01' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS separations_calendar_2026 FROM semantic.separation WHERE effective_month BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-01' AND pay_plan_code = 'ES' GROUP BY agency_subelement_code, agency_subelement ORDER BY separations_twelve_months DESC
```

question_text: Are higher-graded CBP Officers leaving at a higher rate than lower grades?
answer_text:
Exploratory

No. Across the twelve months to August 2026, CBP Officers at GS-13 to GS-15 separated at a rate of 0.034, slightly below the 0.035 for grades 05 to 12. The rate is not higher with grade. The highest rates sit in the lower grades 05 and 07, and grade 15 (0.066, on 181 staff) is the only senior grade above the cell average, on a small base.

| Grade | Separation rate, trailing twelve months to August 2026 |
|---|---|
| 00 | 0.219 (36 at start, small base) |
| 05 | 0.102 |
| 07 | 0.077 |
| 09 | 0.039 |
| 11 | 0.007 |
| 12 | 0.032 |
| 13 | 0.032 |
| 14 | 0.038 |
| 15 | 0.066 (181 at start, small base) |

The cell as a whole is 0.035. No 2025 deferred resignation separations appear in this cell, so the rates with and without that wave are the same. Late reports keep arriving, so recent separations will grow. The grade figures come from a one-off query, not the review's standard calculations, which do not break down by grade. The rate uses the review's definition: separations over the average of the August 2025 and August 2026 headcounts.

I read "higher-graded" as GS-13 and above, and the cell as CBP Officers, trailing twelve months to August 2026. If you meant a different grade cut, or separation counts rather than rates, say so.

```sql
WITH hs AS (
  SELECT grade, count(*) AS n
  FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
  WHERE snapshot_month = '2025-09-01' AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
  GROUP BY grade
),
he AS (
  SELECT grade, count(*) AS n
  FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
  WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01' AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
  GROUP BY grade
),
sp AS (
  SELECT grade, count(*) AS seps, count(*) FILTER (WHERE drp_indicator = 'Y') AS drp_seps
  FROM semantic.separation
  WHERE effective_month BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-01' AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
  GROUP BY grade
)
SELECT COALESCE(hs.grade, he.grade, sp.grade) AS grade,
       hs.n AS headcount_start_2025_09,
       he.n AS headcount_end_2026_08,
       sp.seps AS separations_ttm,
       sp.drp_seps AS drp_separations_ttm
FROM hs
FULL JOIN he ON he.grade = hs.grade
FULL JOIN sp ON sp.grade = COALESCE(hs.grade, he.grade)
ORDER BY grade
```

question_text: Roughly how many CBP Officers could retire in the next five years, going by age bracket and years of service?
answer_text:
Exploratory

About 8,005 CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) on the August 2026 snapshot are at least 45 years old with 20 or more years of service, so they could be retirement-eligible within five years. That is about 29% of the 27,650 officers on the snapshot. Under the usual law-enforcement threshold (age 50 with 20 years), 5,760 are already past it and 2,245 aged 45 to 49 would reach it within the window.

| Age bracket | Officers with 20+ years | Eligible within five years |
|---|---|---|
| 45-49 | 2,245 | Reach age 50 within the window |
| 50-54 | 2,483 | Already eligible |
| 55-59 | 2,130 | Already eligible |
| 60-64 | 850 | Already eligible |
| 65 or more | 297 | Already eligible |

The retirement threshold is my assumption, not a field in the data, which holds no retirement eligibility. The 20+ years band cannot separate 20 to 24 years from 25 or more, so a 25-year rule for officers under 50 is not captured. If everyone aged 45 and over with 10 to 20 years were added, the ceiling would be about 11,400. Every duty-station location in these rows is estimated from job postings, but the headcounts themselves do not depend on location. Late reports keep arriving, so counts can change. I read this as officers' retirement eligibility on the age 50 with 20 years threshold, as of the August 2026 snapshot; if you meant the retirements actually recorded over the past year, or a different threshold, say so.

```sql
SELECT age_bracket,
       CASE WHEN length_of_service_years < 1 THEN '<1'
            WHEN length_of_service_years < 3 THEN '1-3'
            WHEN length_of_service_years < 5 THEN '3-5'
            WHEN length_of_service_years < 10 THEN '5-10'
            WHEN length_of_service_years < 20 THEN '10-20'
            ELSE '20+' END AS service_bucket,
       COUNT(*) AS headcount,
       SUM(CASE WHEN location_imputed THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS location_imputed_rows
FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01'
  AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD'
  AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
GROUP BY age_bracket, service_bucket
ORDER BY age_bracket, service_bucket
```

The analyst supplies this fact, which the data does not contain: The government was shut down from October 1 to November 12, 2025.

Redo that with the shutdown taken out.

CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) landed 475 accessions against a plan of 594 hires in FY2026 Q1 (October to December 2025), a variance of -119 hires (-20.0% of plan). The quarter's accessions are still arriving in later OPM files, so the gap may narrow.
answer_text:
Verified
Assuming, as you state, that no one could be onboarded from October 1 to November 12, 2025, the plan scaled to the days hiring was possible is about 316 hires. Against that scaled plan, the 475 actual accessions land +158.6 hires (+50.1%), compared with -119 hires (-20.0%) against the full plan of 594.

- Days in the quarter: October 1 to December 31, 2025 = 31 + 30 + 31 = 92
- Days hiring could not happen: October 1 to November 12 = 31 + 12 = 43
- Days hiring was possible: 92 - 43 = 49
- Scaled plan: 594 x 49 / 92 = 316.4
- Variance against the scaled plan: 475 - 316.4 = +158.6 hires, or 158.6 / 316.4 = +50.1%

This comparison assumes the shutdown dates you gave; the data does not record them. Later OPM files can add accessions, and accessions by month for October to December 2025 would test the assumption directly if you want that from a one-off query.

question_text: TSA told Congress about 1,110 screeners left during the October and November 2025 shutdown. What does the OPM data show, and how many of those were quits?
answer_text:
Exploratory

question_text: What's the average salary of TSA screeners, and how does it compare with CBP Officers?
answer_text:
Exploratory
TSA screeners (Transportation Security Administration (HSBC), series 1802) had an average annualized basic pay of $74,752 across 46,913 staff in the August 2026 snapshot. CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection (HSBD), series 1895) averaged $104,511 across 27,650 staff, about $29,759 (roughly 40%) more than TSA screeners.
Pay is estimated for nearly all of these rows: 42,225 of the 46,913 TSA screener rows (90%) and all 27,650 CBP Officer rows were imputed from job postings because OPM redacted them, and the imputation test has not been run here. These are simple averages across all staff in each series, so grade and locality mix affects them.
I read "salary" as annualized adjusted basic pay, averaged across all staff in each series on the August 2026 snapshot; if you meant a grade-matched comparison or pay for a different month, say so.

```sql
SELECT agency_subelement_code, occupational_series_code, COUNT(*) AS headcount, AVG(annualized_adjusted_basic_pay)::numeric(12,0) AS avg_basic_pay, SUM(CASE WHEN pay_imputed THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS pay_imputed_rows FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01' AND agency_subelement_code IN ('HSBC', 'HSBD') AND occupational_series_code IN ('1802', '1895') GROUP BY agency_subelement_code, occupational_series_code ORDER BY agency_subelement_code
```

question_text: Do higher-grade CBP Officer postings stay open longer than lower-grade ones?
answer_text:
Exploratory

No, the pattern runs the other way. CBP Officer postings (those listing series 1895) at grades 12 to 15 were advertised for about 6 to 8 days on average, while the grade 5 and grade 9 postings stayed open about 22 to 29 days. Across the 470 postings in the data, the average advertised window was 7.7 days at grade 12, 7.4 at grade 13, 7.2 at grade 14 and 6.4 at grade 15. Grade 5 averaged 29.3 days (14 postings) and grade 9 averaged 22.4 days (22 postings). The window is open date to close date, not time to fill: there are no applicant or hire links, so I can't say how long any posting took to fill. Postings open through October 2026 have close dates still ahead, so their windows are as advertised.

I read this as the advertised window (close date minus open date) for all CBP Officer postings, grouped by minimum grade; if you meant time to fill, or postings open on a particular date, say so.

```sql
SELECT minimum_grade, COUNT(*) AS postings, ROUND(AVG(close_date - open_date), 1) AS avg_days_advertised, percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY close_date - open_date) AS median_days_advertised, MIN(open_date) AS first_open, MAX(open_date) AS last_open FROM semantic.job_posting WHERE occupational_series_codes ? '1895' GROUP BY minimum_grade ORDER BY minimum_grade

question_text: Roughly how many CBP Officers could retire in the next five years, going by age bracket and years of service?
answer_text:
Exploratory

Roughly 10,660 CBP Officers (about 39% of the 27,650 on the August 2026 snapshot) are eligible to retire now or within five years, using a rough eligibility proxy of age 50 with 20 years of service. About 5,760 (21%) already meet that proxy, and about 4,900 more reach it within five years. The data has no retirement-eligibility field, so these are eligibility counts, not a forecast of retirements; the age-by-service cross-tab is in the first query below. The duty station fields behind these rows are estimated from job postings, but this count does not use location.

- Eligible now (age 50 or over with 20 or more years): 5,760.
- Within five years, age 45 to 49 with 20 or more years (they reach age 50 within five years): 2,245.
- Within five years, age 45 or over with 15 to 19 years (they reach 20 years within five years): 2,655.

Late OPM files do not change these snapshot counts. I read "could retire" as eligibility under that proxy, with the proxy as my working assumption, not a rule from the data; if you meant the retirements actually recorded over the last twelve months, or a different eligibility rule, say so.

```sql
SELECT age_bracket,
  SUM(CASE WHEN length_of_service_years < 10 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS under_10_years,
  SUM(CASE WHEN length_of_service_years >= 10 AND length_of_service_years < 20 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS years_10_to_19,
  SUM(CASE WHEN length_of_service_years >= 20 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS years_20_plus,
  COUNT(*) AS total,
  SUM(CASE WHEN location_imputed THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS location_imputed_rows
FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01'
  AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD'
  AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
GROUP BY age_bracket
ORDER BY age_bracket
```

Assuming, as you state, that no one could be onboarded from October 1 to November 12, 2025, the plan scaled to the days hiring was possible is about 316.4 hires, and the 475 actual accessions land 158.6 hires (+50.1%) above it. Against the full plan of 594, the variance was -119 (-20.0%). This is arithmetic on the assumption, not something the data shows: the 475 actual accessions are unchanged, and the scaled plan only reflects the days hiring could occur. Later OPM files can add accessions, and accessions by month for October to December 2025 are the better test of this assumption; a one-off query can pull them.

- Days in the quarter: October 1 to December 31, 2025 = 31 + 30 + 31 = 92
- Days hiring could not happen: October 1 to November 12 = 31 + 12 = 43
- Days hiring was possible: 92 - 43 = 49
- Scaled plan: 594 x 49 / 92 = 316.4
- Variance against the scaled plan: 475 - 316.4 = 158.6, or 158.6 / 316.4 = 50.1%

I read "redo" as the hiring variance for CBP Officers in FY2026 Q1 with the shutdown days removed from the plan; if you meant the raw count against the full plan, that is the -119 figure above.

question_text: What's the average salary of TSA screeners, and how does it compare with CBP Officers?
answer_text:
Exploratory
As of the August 2026 snapshot, TSA screeners (Transportation Security Administration (TSA), series 1802) average $74,752 in annual basic pay, and CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection (CBP), series 1895) average $104,511, so screeners earn about $29,759 (28%) less on average. Both averages are estimated: OPM redacted pay for 42,225 of 46,913 TSA screener rows (90%) and all 27,650 CBP Officer rows, so the figures are filled in from job postings. I read "average salary" as the mean annual basic pay across current staff in the August 2026 snapshot; if you meant median pay, or pay for FY2026 Q1, say so.

question_text: How many postings listed the Border Patrol series 1896 between September 2025 and October 2026, counting ones that list several series?
answer_text:
Exploratory

889 job postings listed the Border Patrol Agent series (1896) with an open date between September 1, 2025 and October 31, 2026, counting postings that also list other series. Each posting has a distinct control number, so none is counted twice. Postings cover announcements opened only through that window, so this is the count opened in it, not a count of hires.

question_text: Do higher-grade CBP Officer postings stay open longer than lower-grade ones?
answer_text:
Exploratory

Higher-grade CBP Officer postings do not stay open longer. Postings advertised at GS-9 and at GS-5 to 7 stayed open about 29 days on average, while single-grade postings at GS-12 to GS-15 averaged 6 to 8 days. The windows cover CBP Officer (1895) postings opened September 2025 to October 2026, and the 13 postings at GS-13 to 14 and the three at GS-13 to 14 mixed averaged 17.7 days.

| Advertised grade (single grade) | Postings | Average days open |
|---|---|---|
| 9 | 13 | 29.2 |
| 12 | 55 | 7.7 |
| 13 | 208 | 7.3 |
| 14 | 127 | 7.2 |
| 15 | 32 | 6.4 |

These are posting windows (open date to close date), not time to fill, and the postings cannot be linked to the people hired through them, so late-filled or cancelled postings are not visible. I read this as the open-to-close window of CBP Officer postings by advertised grade; if you meant how long each vacancy took to fill, that is not available in the data.

```sql
SELECT minimum_grade, maximum_grade, COUNT(*) AS postings, ROUND(AVG(close_date - open_date), 1) AS avg_days_open, MIN(close_date - open_date) AS min_days_open, MAX(close_date - open_date) AS max_days_open FROM semantic.job_posting WHERE occupational_series_codes ? '1895' AND open_date BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-10-31' GROUP BY minimum_grade, maximum_grade ORDER BY minimum_grade, maximum_grade
```

question_text: When in the year do CBP Officers retire? Show retirements by month.

Exploratory
CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) retired most in December 2025, with 152 of 586 retirements over the twelve months from September 2025 to August 2026. The other months ran between 24 and 54 in the autumn and early winter, then 26 to 52 from January to August 2026. None of these retirements came through the 2025 deferred resignation program. question_text: Which DHS components lost the most senior executives this year?
answer_text:
Exploratory

DHS Headquarters lost the most Senior Executive Service staff in the twelve months from September 2025 to August 2026, with 57 separations. FEMA (HSCB) had 44 and ICE (HSBB) had 37. The full ranking is below.

| Component | Senior executive separations |
|---|---|
| DHS Headquarters (HSAA) | 57 |
| FEMA (HSCB) | 44 |
| ICE (HSBB) | 37 |
| CBP (HSBD) | 31 |
| USCIS (HSAB) | 30 |
| CISA (HSCA) | 27 |
| U.S. Secret Service (HSAD) | 23 |
| S&T (HSFA) | 8 |
| U.S. Coast Guard civilian (HSAC) | 7 |
| FLETC (HSBE) | 4 |
| Domestic Nuclear Detection Office (HSDA) | 3 |
| OIG (HSAE) | 2 |

These are counts across all separation categories, and the total is 273. They include the 2025 deferred resignation wave, which I did not split out, and they are not rates. Larger components with more executives will tend to rank higher, so a rate would be the fairer comparison. The Domestic Nuclear Detection Office is outside the review's twelve components but is included in the total. I read "this year" as the twelve months to August 2026 and "senior executives" as the Senior Executive Service (pay plan ES); if you meant calendar 2026 only, or the separation rate, say so.

```sql
SELECT s.agency_subelement_code, s.agency_subelement, COUNT(*) AS senior_executive_separations
FROM semantic.separation s
WHERE s.effective_month BETWEEN DATE '2025-09-01' AND DATE '2026-08-01'
  AND s.pay_plan_code = 'ES'
GROUP BY s.agency_subelement_code, s.agency_subelement
ORDER BY senior_executive_separations DESC
```

question_text: Are higher-graded CBP Officers leaving at a higher rate than lower grades?
answer_text:
Exploratory

No. Lower grades in this cell leave at higher rates than the bulk of higher grades. Grade 05 CBP Officers separated at 0.102 and grade 07 at 0.077 over the twelve months to August 2026, against 0.032 for grade 12 (about 17,000 officers) and 0.032 for grade 13. Grades 14 and 15 are at 0.038 and 0.066, but grade 15 rests on about 180 officers and 12 separations, so that figure is noisy. Across all grades the rate was 954 separations on an average headcount of about 27,150, or 0.035. No separations in this window carry the 2025 deferred resignation program flag, so the rates with and without that wave are the same. Late reports keep arriving, so these counts will grow slightly.

I read "higher-graded" as the grade-by-grade separation rate for CBP Officers over the trailing twelve months to August 2026; if you meant the count of separations by grade, or the rate for grade bands such as 12 to 13 versus 14 and above, say so.

```sql
WITH sep AS (
  SELECT grade, COUNT(*) AS separations, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE drp_indicator = 'N') AS separations_excl_drp
  FROM semantic.separation
  WHERE effective_month BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-01' AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
  GROUP BY grade
),
hc_start AS (
  SELECT grade, COUNT(*) AS headcount_start FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
  WHERE snapshot_month = '2025-09-01' AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
  GROUP BY grade
),
hc_end AS (
  SELECT grade, COUNT(*) AS headcount_end FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
  WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01' AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
  GROUP BY grade
)
SELECT COALESCE(s.grade, a.grade, e.grade) AS grade, a.headcount_start, e.headcount_end, s.separations, s.separations_excl_drp,
  ROUND(s.separations::numeric / NULLIF((a.headcount_start + e.headcount_end) / 2.0, 0), 4) AS rate,
  ROUND(s.separations_excl_drp::numeric / NULLIF((a.headcount_start + e.headcount_end) / 2.0, 0), 4) AS rate_excl_drp
FROM sep s
FULL OUTER JOIN hc_start a ON a.grade = s.grade
FULL OUTER JOIN hc_end e ON e.grade = COALESCE(s.grade, a.grade)
ORDER BY COALESCE(s.grade, a.grade, e.grade)
```

question_text: Roughly how many CBP Officers could retire in the next five years, going by age bracket and years of service?
answer_text:
Exploratory

Roughly 5,760 CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) were aged 50 or over with 20 or more years of service as of the August 2026 snapshot, about 21% of the 27,650 officers on staff. Of those, 3,277 are already 55 or older, and the 2,483 aged 50 to 54 will reach 55 within the five-year window. Officers aged 45 to 49 with 20 or more years (2,245) reach 50 within five years, so the pool could grow to about 8,000 if the age-50 threshold applies. Eligibility rules are not a field in the data, so the age-50 and 20-year threshold is my assumption, not an OPM figure. These are people who could retire, not a forecast of who will. Past retirement counts would show the likely share.

I read "could retire" as officers aged 50 or over with 20 or more years of service; if you meant the count of retirement separations, or a different age or service threshold, say so.

```sql
SELECT age_bracket,
       CASE WHEN length_of_service_years >= 20 THEN '20+ years'
            WHEN length_of_service_years >= 10 THEN '10-20 years'
            WHEN length_of_service_years >= 5 THEN '5-10 years'

WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01'
  AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD'
  AND occupational_series_code = '1895'

ORDER BY 1, 2

Against that scaled plan, the 475 actual accessions land 159 hires over (+50.1%), compared with 119 hires under (-20.0%) against the full plan of 594. The actuals are unchanged, and the scaling only changes the plan.

- Days in the quarter: October 1 to December 31, 2025 = 31 + 30 + 31 = 92
- Days hiring could not happen: October 1 to November 12 = 31 + 12 = 43
- Days hiring was possible: 92 - 43 = 49
- Scaled plan: 594 x 49 / 92 = 316.4
- Variance against the scaled plan: 475 - 316.4 = +158.6, or 158.6 / 316.4 = +50.1%

This comparison does not show that the shutdown explains the shortfall. Later OPM files can add accessions, so these figures will shift. question_text: Do higher-grade CBP Officer postings stay open longer than lower-grade ones?
answer_text:
Exploratory

No, the pattern runs the other way: among CBP Officer (1895) postings opened from September 2025 to October 2026, the lower-grade postings stayed open longer. Grade 5 postings had a median open window of 30 days and grade 9 postings 28 days, while grades 12 to 15 had a median of 6 days. These are the posting windows as advertised (open to close date), not time to fill. The data has no applicant records and no link from a posting to the people hired through it, so it cannot show how long a posting took to fill. The grade 5 and grade 9 groups are small (14 and 22 postings), and grades 12 to 15 are the bulk of the postings (427 of 469 with a stated grade).

I read this as the advertised open-to-close window by minimum grade across all CBP Officer postings opened in that span; if you meant time to fill, or postings open on a particular date, say so.

```sql
SELECT minimum_grade, COUNT(*) AS postings, percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY close_date - open_date) AS median_days, ROUND(AVG(close_date - open_date), 1) AS avg_days, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE close_date - open_date > 30) AS over_30_days, SUM(COALESCE(total_openings, 0)) AS known_openings FROM semantic.job_posting WHERE occupational_series_codes ? '1895' AND open_date >= '2025-09-01' AND open_date <= '2026-10-31' AND minimum_grade IN ('5', '9', '11', '12', '13', '14', '15') GROUP BY minimum_grade ORDER BY minimum_grade::int
```

question_text: When in the year do CBP Officers retire? Show retirements by month.
answer_text:
Exploratory

CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) recorded 586 retirements over the twelve months from September 2025 to August 2026. December 2025 is the peak month at 152, about 26% of the total, and the other months run between 24 and 54 until a steady 31 to 52 from April to August 2026. These counts include all three retirement categories (voluntary, early out, and other). Late reports keep arriving, so the most recent months, especially August 2026, will grow. I read "when in the year" as the monthly count of retirements over the trailing twelve months; if you meant the retirement rate, or retirements for a single year, say so.

```sql
SELECT to_char(m.month, 'YYYY-MM') AS month, COUNT(s.*) AS retirements
FROM generate_series(DATE '2025-09-01', DATE '2026-08-01', INTERVAL '1 month') AS m(month)

  AND s.occupational_series_code = '1895'

GROUP BY m.month
ORDER BY m.month
```

Higher-graded CBP Officers did not leave at a consistently higher rate over the twelve months to August 2026. GS-13 to GS-15 and the Senior Executive grade together separated at 0.035, while GS-05 to GS-09 separated at 0.064, and GS-11 to GS-13 were lowest.

| GS-14 | 850 | 32 | 0.038 |

The top grades rest on small bases (181 at GS-15, 32 in the Senior Executive grade), so a few departures move those rates a lot. No separation in this window carries the 2025 deferred resignation flag, so the rates with and without that wave are identical. Late reports keep arriving, so these counts will grow slightly. Each rate uses the grade's headcount at the September 2025 and August 2026 snapshots, so people who changed grade during the year count in both.

I read "higher-graded" as GS-13 through GS-15 and the Senior Executive grade, against GS-05 through GS-09, on the trailing twelve-month rate to August 2026; if you meant the grade-by-grade pattern, the table above answers that, or if you meant the count of separations, say so.

question_text: Roughly how many CBP Officers could retire in the next five years, going by age bracket and years of service?
answer_text:
Exploratory

Using the August 2026 snapshot, about 6,190 CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) are already eligible to retire under an assumed rule, and about 1,840 more will reach eligibility by August 2031. That is roughly 8,030 of 27,650 officers, or about 29%. Eligibility is not the same as retirement. The eligibility rule is my assumption, not something in the data: age 50 with 20 years of service, or 25 years at any age, the usual law-enforcement retirement terms. Please check it against the current OPM rules before quoting.

| Group (assumed eligibility) | Officers |
|---|---|
| Age 50 to 54, 20+ years | 2,483 |
| Age 55 to 59, 20+ years | 2,130 |
| Age 60 to 64, 20+ years | 850 |
| Age 65 or more, 20+ years | 297 |
| Under 50, 25+ years | 433 |
| **Eligible now** | **6,193** |
| Age 45 to 49, 20 to 24 years (reach age 50 by 2031) | 1,838 |

This is a floor for the five-year figure. Officers aged 45 to 49 with 15 to 19 years of service could also cross both thresholds by 2031, but the service bands in the data do not separate them, so they are not counted. I read "could retire" as eligibility under that rule; if you meant the count of retirements actually recorded, I can pull those from the separation categories.

```sql
SELECT age_bracket,
       CASE WHEN length_of_service_years < 20 THEN 'under 20 years'
            WHEN length_of_service_years < 25 THEN '20 to 24 years'
            WHEN length_of_service_years < 30 THEN '25 to 29 years'
            ELSE '30 years or more' END AS service_band,
       COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01'
  AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD'
  AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2
```

Assuming, as you state, that no one could be onboarded from October 1 to November 12, 2025, the plan scaled to the days hiring was possible is about 316 hires. Against that scaled plan, the 475 actual CBP Officer accessions in FY2026 Q1 (October to December 2025) land 158.6 hires (50.1%) above plan, compared with 119 hires (20.0%) below the full plan of 594.

- Days hiring could not happen: October 1 to November 12 = 31 + 12 = 43
- Days hiring was possible: 92 - 43 = 49
- Scaled plan: 594 × 49 / 92 = 316.4

As of the August 2026 snapshot, the largest estimated duty-station concentrations of CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) are Washington, District of Columbia (1,956), Sterling, Virginia (790), and Ashburn, Virginia (645), out of 27,650 officers across 189 cities. SELECT duty_station_city, duty_station_state, COUNT(*) AS headcount, SUM(CASE WHEN location_imputed THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS imputed_rows, SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER () AS total_headcount FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01' AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895' GROUP BY duty_station_city, duty_station_state ORDER BY headcount DESC

question_text: Do higher-grade CBP Officer postings stay open longer than lower-grade ones?
answer_text:
Exploratory

No. In CBP Officer (1895) postings opened September 2025 to October 2026, lower-grade postings stayed open longer, not higher-grade ones. Postings at GS-9 averaged 29.2 days open, against 7.7 for GS-12, 7.3 for GS-13, 5.8 for GS-14 and 6.4 for GS-15. The GS-13 average includes at least one window of 181 days, but the pattern holds. The GS-5 to 7 postings (29.2 days) and the GS-9 to 12 postings (13.6 days) are also longer than the single-grade postings above GS-12.

These are posting windows, from open date to close date, not how long a vacancy took to fill. Postings are not linked to the people hired through them, and postings filled or cancelled early are not visible, so these windows cannot show time to hire. The higher-grade groups have 126 to 208 postings each, but the GS-5 to 7 and GS-9 groups have only 13 each, so treat those figures as thin. I read "stay open longer" as the posting window for CBP Officer postings; if you meant time until filled, say so, though that is not available in the data.

```sql
SELECT minimum_grade, maximum_grade, COUNT(*) AS postings, ROUND(AVG(close_date - open_date), 1) AS avg_days_open, ROUND(AVG(total_openings), 1) AS avg_openings FROM semantic.job_posting WHERE occupational_series_codes ? '1895' AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND open_date BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-10-31' GROUP BY minimum_grade, maximum_grade ORDER BY minimum_grade, maximum_grade
```

question_text: Which DHS components lost the most senior executives this year?

Rates are separations divided by the average of the September 2025 and August 2026 headcounts, the same basis as the standard rate. The overall rate for the cell is 0.035, and no separations in this cell carry the 2025 deferred resignation flag, so the rate with and without that wave is the same. Late reports keep arriving, so recent counts will grow. The grade mix shifts sharply between the two snapshots (grade 05 rose from 412 to 898, grade 07 from 863 to 1,234), so check grade coding before quoting grade-level rates.

question_text: Roughly how many CBP Officers could retire in the next five years, going by age bracket and years of service?
answer_text:
Exploratory

About 4,970 CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) are eligible to retire by August 2031, or could become eligible, under standard federal retirement rules, based on the August 2026 snapshot. That is a rough estimate: the upper bound is about 5,030, and the age and service figures are in five-year and service-band groups, so the boundaries are approximate. Eligibility is not a forecast of departures; the data has no retirement plan or intent field.

- Already eligible or reaching eligibility: 60 to 64 with 5+ years (1,046), 65 and over with 5+ years (347), 55 to 59 with 15+ years (2,463), and 50 to 54 with 25+ years (1,110). Total 4,966.
- Upper bound: adds 55 to 59 with 5 to 15 years (67), which reach age 62 only partway through the window.
- CBP Officers are often under law-enforcement retirement rules (age 50 with 20 years, or 25 years at any age). The data does not record retirement plan, so I cannot split by it. Under those rules, at least 5,760 officers (age 50 and over with 20+ years) are eligible now, before counting those under 50 with 25+ years.

The counts do not use location, though the underlying rows carry estimated location flags.

I read "could retire" as eligibility under standard federal retirement rules through August 2031; if you meant actual retirement separations over the past year, say so.

```sql
SELECT age_bracket,
       CASE WHEN length_of_service_years < 1 THEN '<1'
            WHEN length_of_service_years < 3 THEN '1-3'
            WHEN length_of_service_years < 5 THEN '3-5'
            WHEN length_of_service_years < 10 THEN '5-10'
            WHEN length_of_service_years < 20 THEN '10-20'
            ELSE '20+' END AS service_bucket,
       COUNT(*) AS headcount,
       SUM(CASE WHEN location_imputed THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS location_imputed_rows
FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01'
  AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD'
  AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
GROUP BY age_bracket, service_bucket
ORDER BY age_bracket, service_bucket
```

```sql
SELECT age_bracket,

question_text: How many postings listed the Border Patrol series 1896 between September 2025 and October 2026, counting ones that list several series?
answer_text:
Exploratory

889 USAJOBS postings listed Border Patrol Agent (series 1896) among their occupational series, with an open date between September 1, 2025 and October 31, 2026. Each posting has a unique control number, so none is double-counted. This counts postings that list 1896 alongside other series, as you asked. Postings are counted by open date, and the window matches the full span of the postings data.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS postings, COUNT(DISTINCT control_number) AS distinct_control_numbers FROM semantic.job_posting WHERE occupational_series_codes ? '1896' AND open_date BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-10-31'
```

question_text: Do higher-grade CBP Officer postings stay open longer than lower-grade ones?
answer_text:
Exploratory

No. Higher-grade CBP Officer postings did not stay open longer. Announcements opened from September 2025 to October 2026 averaged 5.8 days from open to close at GS-14 and 6.4 at GS-15, against 7.4 at GS-13 and 7.7 at GS-12. The lowest grades had the longest windows: 29.3 days at GS-5 and 22.4 at GS-9.

Late reports do not apply here, but these are announced windows (open date to close date), not how long a posting stayed open in practice or time to hire. Postings filled or cancelled early are not reflected, and the records have no applicant data to link postings to hires. The six postings with grade "00" are too few to read.

I read "higher-grade" as the lowest grade on the posting and "stay open longer" as the announced open-to-close window; if you meant the highest grade or the actual time a posting stayed open, say so.

```sql
SELECT minimum_grade, COUNT(*) AS postings, ROUND(AVG(close_date - open_date)::numeric, 1) AS avg_window_days, MIN(close_date - open_date) AS min_window_days, MAX(close_date - open_date) AS max_window_days FROM semantic.job_posting WHERE agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_codes ? '1895' AND open_date BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-10-31' GROUP BY minimum_grade ORDER BY LPAD(minimum_grade, 2, '0')
```

question_text: When in the year do CBP Officers retire? Show retirements by month.
answer_text:
Exploratory

CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) retired 586 times over the twelve months from September 2025 to August 2026, and December 2025 was the peak at 152, about a quarter of the year's total. Outside December, the monthly count ran between 24 and 54 until April to July 2026, when it held between 45 and 52.

| Month | Retirements |
|---|---|
| 2025-09 | 54 |
| 2025-10 | 36 |
| 2025-11 | 24 |
| 2025-12 | 152 |
| 2026-01 | 44 |
| 2026-02 | 26 |
| 2026-03 | 31 |
| 2026-04 | 45 |
| 2026-05 | 52 |
| 2026-06 | 46 |
| 2026-07 | 45 |
| 2026-08 | 31 |

None of these retirements came through the 2025 deferred resignation program. Late reports keep arriving, so the most recent months will grow slightly. I read "retire" as all three retirement categories (voluntary, early out, and other) over the twelve months the data covers; if you meant the trailing twelve months to August 2026 as a rate, or only voluntary retirements, say so.

```sql
SELECT effective_month, COUNT(*) AS retirements, SUM(CASE WHEN drp_indicator = 'Y' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS drp_retirements FROM semantic.separation WHERE effective_month BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-01' AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND occupational_series_code = '1895' AND separation_category LIKE 'RETIREMENT%' GROUP BY effective_month ORDER BY effective_month
```

question_text: How many CBP Officers who left this year had less than one year of service?
answer_text:
Exploratory
Of the CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895) who separated in the twelve months from September 2025 to August 2026, 170 had less than one year of service. Of those, 138 separated in calendar 2026 (January to August). By category, 76 were quits, 78 were other separations, 14 were terminations, and 2 were transfers out. Late reports keep arriving, so these counts will grow slightly. I summed the monthly rows from the one-off query to reach 170 and 138. I read "this year" as the trailing twelve months to August 2026, the period the data covers, and "left" as all separation categories, with service measured at separation. If you meant calendar 2026 only, use 138; if you meant quits only, say so.

```sql
SELECT s.effective_month, s.separation_category, s.length_of_service_years, COUNT(*) AS separations FROM semantic.separation s WHERE s.effective_month BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-01' AND s.agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD' AND s.occupational_series_code = '1895' AND s.length_of_service_years < 1 GROUP BY s.effective_month, s.separation_category, s.length_of_service_years ORDER BY s.effective_month
```

question_text: Which DHS components lost the most senior executives this year?
answer_text:
Exploratory

DHS Headquarters (HSAA) lost the most Senior Executive Service staff (pay plan ES) over the twelve months September 2025 to August 2026, with 57 separations, ahead of FEMA (HSCB) with 44 and ICE (HSBB) with 37. Calendar 2026 (January to August) leads with DHS Headquarters at 29, then ICE at 21 and FEMA and CBP at 18 each. Late reports keep arriving, so recent counts will grow. The 2025 deferred resignation program accounts for much of FEMA's and DHS Headquarters' totals: excluding it, DHS Headquarters leads with 42, then ICE with 37, CBP with 31, the Secret Service with 23, and FEMA and USCIS with 21 each. TSA (HSBC) does not appear in the results, so none are recorded for it in this pay plan. Three separations sit under HSDA, a code outside the twelve-component list. These are counts, not rates, because I did not have senior executive headcounts by component. I read "senior executives" as the Senior Executive Service and "this year" as the twelve months to August 2026; if you meant a rate, or only calendar 2026, say so.

SELECT agency_subelement_code, COUNT(*) AS senior_executive_separations, SUM(CASE WHEN drp_indicator = 'Y' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS drp_separations, SUM(CASE WHEN effective_month >= DATE '2026-01-01' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS calendar_2026_separations FROM semantic.separation WHERE effective_month BETWEEN DATE '2025-09-01' AND DATE '2026-08-01' AND pay_plan_code = 'ES' AND occupational_series_code IS NOT NULL GROUP BY agency_subelement_code ORDER BY senior_executive_separations DESC

question_text: Are higher-graded CBP Officers leaving at a higher rate than lower grades?
answer_text:
Exploratory

For CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, 1895), the separation rate over the trailing twelve months to August 2026 was 0.0337 for GS-13 to GS-15 and 0.0352 for GS-05 to GS-12. The higher grades are not leaving faster as a group. Within the bands, GS-15 (0.0663, 12 separations) and the Senior Executive Service (0.2188, 7 separations on about 32 people) run higher, but those bases are small. No separations in this cell carry the 2025 deferred resignation indicator, so the rates with and without it are the same. Late reports keep arriving, so recent counts will grow. Headcount shifts sharply between the September 2025 and August 2026 snapshots in GS-05 to GS-07 (GS-05 goes from 412 to 898), so those rates depend heavily on the denominator.

Rate = separations ÷ average of the September 2025 and August 2026 headcounts. Grade-band totals: GS-05 to GS-12 is 767 separations on about 21,771 average headcount; GS-13 to GS-15 is 180 on 5,344.

question_text: Roughly how many CBP Officers could retire in the next five years, going by age bracket and years of service?
answer_text:
Exploratory

About 8,000 CBP Officers (Customs and Border Protection, series 1895) could retire within five years, on the August 2026 snapshot of 27,650 officers. I applied a simple eligibility rule that is not in the data: age 50 with 20 years of service. Of the 8,005, 5,760 already meet it (age 50 and over with 20 or more years) and 2,245 more (ages 45 to 49 with 20 or more years) will meet it by 2031.

This counts eligibility, not expected retirements, and it leaves out officers who qualify at any age with 25 years, because the service bands do not split 20 to 24 from 25 to 29 years. The true pool is therefore somewhat larger. Duty station is estimated for these rows, but the age and service counts are published and do not depend on location.

I read "could retire" as the eligibility pool under that rule. If you meant expected retirements, say so, and I can pull the retirement separations for CBP Officers over the past twelve months as the nearest measure.

```sql
SELECT age_bracket,
       CASE WHEN length_of_service_years < 20 THEN 'under 20 years'
            WHEN length_of_service_years < 30 THEN '20 to 29 years'
            ELSE '30 or more years' END AS service_band,
       COUNT(*) AS headcount,
       SUM(CASE WHEN location_imputed THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS location_imputed_rows
FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01'
  AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD'
  AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2
```

question_text: How many postings listed the Border Patrol series 1896 between September 2025 and October 2026, counting ones that list several series?
answer_text:
Exploratory
889 USAJOBS postings listing the Border Patrol Agent series (1896) opened between September 1, 2025 and October 31, 2026, counting postings that list several series. Each control number appears once, so the 889 postings are 889 distinct announcements. This counts announcements by their open date, and postings filled or cancelled early are still included, so it is a count of advertisements rather than of people hired.

SELECT COUNT(*) AS postings, COUNT(DISTINCT control_number) AS distinct_control_numbers FROM semantic.job_posting WHERE occupational_series_codes ? '1896' AND open_date >= '2025-09-01' AND open_date <= '2026-10-31'
```

question_text: Do higher-grade CBP Officer postings stay open longer than lower-grade ones?
answer_text:
Exploratory
No. Across the CBP Officer (series 1895) postings opened September 2025 to October 2026, the higher-grade postings had shorter announced windows: GS-7 and GS-9 postings averaged about 29 days open, while GS-11 to GS-15 averaged 6 to 8 days. The 13 GS-7 and 14 GS-9 postings are the only ones at about 29 days, and the 210 GS-13 and 130 GS-14 postings averaged 7.3 and 7.5 days.

The window is the gap between each posting's open and close dates, not how long a job stayed unfilled. The records do not link postings to hires, so time to fill is not available. The query matched every posting that lists series 1895, not only those advertised by CBP, and the six grade "00" postings (13.3 days) have no numbered grade. I read "stay open longer" as the average open-to-close window by maximum grade; if you meant time to fill, or a different grade measure, say so.

```sql
SELECT maximum_grade, COUNT(*) AS postings, ROUND(AVG(close_date - open_date), 1) AS avg_window_days, MIN(close_date - open_date) AS min_window_days, MAX(close_date - open_date) AS max_window_days FROM semantic.job_posting WHERE occupational_series_codes ? '1895' AND open_date BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-10-31' GROUP BY maximum_grade ORDER BY maximum_grade
```

question_text: When in the year do CBP Officers retire? Show retirements by month.
answer_text:
Exploratory

question_text: Roughly how many CBP Officers could retire in the next five years, going by age bracket and years of service?
answer_text:
Exploratory

About 10,660 of the 27,650 CBP Officers on the August 2026 snapshot (roughly 39%) could be retirement-eligible by August 2031. Of these, 5,760 already are, and about 4,900 become eligible within five years. I used the law-enforcement threshold of age 50 with 20 years of service as the test. The age and service bands cannot isolate the separate route of any age with 25 years, so the count is a floor. At most 699 more officers aged 40 to 44 with 20 or more years could qualify on that route. Eligibility is not a forecast of departures, and the records have no retirement intent.

I read this as CBP Officers on the August 2026 snapshot, with eligibility under the age-50, 20-year rule. If you meant actual retirements, I can give the retirement separations for the trailing twelve months.

```sql
SELECT age_bracket,
       CASE WHEN length_of_service_years < 10 THEN 'under 10 years'
            WHEN length_of_service_years < 15 THEN '10 to 14 years'
            WHEN length_of_service_years < 20 THEN '15 to 19 years'
            ELSE '20 or more years' END AS service_band,
       COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM semantic.workforce_snapshot
WHERE snapshot_month = '2026-08-01'
  AND agency_subelement_code = 'HSBD'
  AND occupational_series_code = '1895'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2
```

Arithmetic from the returned rows:
- Already eligible (age 50 or over, 20 or more years): 2,483 + 2,130 + 850 + 297 = 5,760
- Become eligible within five years:
  - Ages 45 to 49 with 20 or more years: 2,245
  - Ages 45 to 49 with 15 to 19 years: 1,330
  - Ages 50 to 54 with 15 to 19 years: 767
  - Ages 55 to 59 with 15 to 19 years: 333
  - Ages 60 to 64 with 15 to 19 years: 176
  - Ages 65 or more with 15 to 19 years: 49
  - Subtotal: 4,900
- Total: 5,760 + 4,900 = 10,660
- Total CBP Officers in the snapshot: 27,650, so 10,660 / 27,650 is about 39%.
